Lug fights in the battle and faces Balor.
Lug casts a sling stone that drives Balor's eye through the back of his head, so that it is Balor's own host that looks upon it.

object_literal: Samildánach — master of all the arts together

The Morrígan aids the Túatha Dé Danann and proclaims the victory.

object_literal: proclaims the victory across Ireland and prophesies

object_literal: promises to take Indech's heart's blood and the kidneys of his valour

statement: The birth and battle take place on Coatepec.

Coyolxauhqui is a daughter of Coatlicue who urges her brothers, the Centzon Huitznahua, to kill their mother.
Coyolxauhqui leads the attack on Coatepec.
Huitzilopochtli is born fully armed, with shield, darts and dart-thrower.
Huitzilopochtli is the child Coatlicue conceives at Coatepec.

object_literal: war; sun; patron of the Mexica
statement: INAH calls Huitzilopochtli the solar god of war and patron of the Mexica.
Huitzilopochtli beheads Coyolxauhqui and her body falls down the side of Coatepec.

object_literal: the Centzon Huitznahua, scattered from Coatepec

object_literal: a great wizard of Tollan

object_literal: Titlacauan

object_literal: rain and agriculture

object_literal: a chariot drawn by two cats

Freyja's dwelling is Fólkvangr.

object_literal: half of the slain
statement: Whenever Freyja rides to battle she gets half the slain, and Odin the other half.
Njörðr's son is Freyr.

object_literal: rain, sunshine and the fruitfulness of the earth

Freyr and Freyja are the children of Njörðr.

object_literal: his sword, as the price of winning Gerðr

Frigg is Odin's wife and knows all fates, though she does not prophesy.
Heimdallr lives at Himinbjörg by Bifröst.
Heimdallr has the horn Gjallarhorn, whose blast is heard in all worlds.

object_literal: son of nine mothers, who were sisters
statement: Heimdallr is called the son of nine mothers, who were sisters.

object_literal: sleepless watcher with keen sight and hearing
statement: He needs less sleep than a bird, sees a hundred leagues by night, and hears grass and wool growing.

object_literal: watchman of the gods
statement: Heimdallr is the watchman of the gods, guarding the bridge against the mountain-giants.
Njörðr lives in heaven at the place called Nóatún.

object_literal: raised in Vanaheim; hostage to the Æsir
statement: Njörðr was brought up in Vanaheim and given to the Æsir as a hostage.

object_literal: wind, sea and seafaring
statement: Njörðr rules the motion of the wind, calms sea and fire, and is invoked for voyages and fishing.
Odin and his brothers Vili and Vé, the sons of Borr, kill the giant Ymir.
Odin and his brothers shape the world from Ymir's body.

object_literal: boldest of the gods; one-handed
statement: Týr is the boldest and most valiant of the gods, and he is one-handed.
As a pledge while the wolf is bound, Týr puts his right hand in Fenrir's mouth; when the wolf is not released it bites the hand off.
Ymir's body becomes the material of the world.

object_literal: formed where rime met heat in Ginnungagap
statement: Ymir arises in Ginnungagap where rime from the north meets heat from the south.

object_literal: earth, sea, rocks and sky made from Ymir's body
statement: From Ymir's flesh the earth is made, from his blood the sea and lakes, from his bones the rocks, and from his skull the sky.

object_literal: Name only in a post-conversion chronicle; no function or myth stated.

Mokosh is one of the idols Volodimer sets up on the Kyiv hill, to which people make offerings.
In 988 Volodimer orders the idols overthrown; Perun's image is tied to a horse's tail, beaten with sticks, dragged down the hill and thrown into the Dnieper.
Perun heads the 980 list of idols on the Kyiv hill.
The 980 annal records Volodimer setting up idols on the hill outside the palace hall in Kyiv.

Enki eats the plants that have grown and falls ill under Ninhursaĝa's curse.
Enlil receives Nanna-Suen and grants him abundance to take back to Urim.
Gilgameš resolves to set off for the mountains.
Ḫuwawa is the guardian Gilgameš sets out to confront.
Nanna-Suen travels to Nibru, the city of his father Enlil.
Nanna-Suen sets his mind on his father's city, loads a boat with gifts and travels to Nibru.
The journey's destination is Nibru (Nippur).
After Enki eats the plants, Ninhursaĝa curses him so that he falls ill; later she brings forth deities to heal the ailing parts of his body.
Ninhursaĝa brings forth deities who heal the ailing parts of Enki's body.
Utu accepts Gilgameš's tears as a gift and grants him seven warriors to guide him.
Enkidu urges that Utu should be told of the expedition, since the mountains are Utu's concern.

object_literal: World Heritage property 1118, inscribed 2005

object_literal: fertility

UNESCO describes the Osun Sacred Grove as the abode of Osun, a Yoruba goddess of fertility, its landscape and river dotted with sanctuaries, shrines, sculptures and artworks in her honour.
Ahura Mazda makes the sixteen good lands.
Ahura Mazda says the first of the good lands he created was Airyana Vaejah, by the good river Daitya.

object_literal: counter-creates the serpent in the river and winter
statement: Then Angra Mainyu, who is all death, counter-creates the serpent in the river and winter, a work of the daevas.
Angra Mainyu sets a counter-creation against each land.
Throughout Videvdad 1 every good land made by Ahura Mazda is answered by a plague from Angra Mainyu.

object_literal: sixteen lands, each answered by a counter-created plague
statement: The list continues land by land — the second, the plains of the Sughdhas, is answered by the locust — until sixteen lands and sixteen plagues are named.
The Mihr Yasht is Yasht 10 of the Avesta.

object_literal: the contract and the given word
statement: The one who lies to Mithra — who breaks the contract — brings death to the whole land; the contract must be kept with the faithful and the unfaithful alike.
Ahura Mazda tells Zarathustra that when he created Mithra, lord of wide pastures, he made him as worthy of sacrifice and prayer as himself.

object_literal: a thousand ears and ten thousand eyes
statement: Mithra is truth-speaking, a chief in assemblies, with a thousand ears and ten thousand eyes.

object_literal: reaches over Hara before the swift-horsed sun
statement: He is the first of the heavenly gods to reach over Mount Hara, before the undying swift-horsed sun.

object_literal: lord of wide pastures
statement: The hymn repeatedly calls Mithra 'lord of wide pastures'.

object_literal: religious geography, not migration history; identifications partial
statement: Darmesteter argues the chapter is a religious geography of Iran mixing mythic lands and real countries, not a record of migrations; only some lands can be identified.

object_literal: dreams that his life is threatened
statement: Baldr dreams ominous dreams threatening his life, and the Æsir resolve to secure protection for him against every danger.

object_literal: takes oaths from all things not to harm Baldr
statement: Frigg takes oaths from fire, water, metals, stones, earth, trees, sicknesses, beasts, birds, poisons and snakes not to harm Baldr.

object_literal: learns of the unsworn mistletoe and pulls it up
statement: Disguised as a woman, Loki learns from Frigg that the young mistletoe west of Valhöll swore no oath, and pulls it up.
Guided by Loki, the blind Höðr throws the mistletoe, which pierces Baldr and kills him.

object_literal: grieves most, understanding the loss best
statement: Odin bears Baldr's death most heavily of all the gods, understanding best what a loss it is for the Æsir.

object_literal: rides Sleipnir to Hel to ransom Baldr
statement: At Frigg's request Hermóðr the Bold, Odin's son, mounts Sleipnir and rides to Hel to ransom Baldr.

object_literal: dies of grief and is burned with Baldr on Hringhorni
statement: At Baldr's ship-funeral his wife Nanna dies of grief and is burned beside him, while Odin lays the ring Draupnir on the pyre.

object_literal: rides nine nights to the Gjallarbrú
statement: Hermóðr rides nine nights through dark valleys to the Gjallarbrú, where the maiden Móðguðr tells him the road to Hel lies downward and north.

object_literal: will release Baldr only if all things weep for him
statement: Hel agrees to release Baldr only if all things in the world, living and dead, weep for him; if any refuses, he stays.

object_literal: all things weep for Baldr at the gods' request
statement: The Æsir send messengers through the world, and men, beasts, earth, stones, trees and metals all weep for Baldr.

object_literal: as the giantess Þökk refuses to weep for Baldr
statement: A giantess named Þökk, believed to be Loki, alone refuses to weep for Baldr, so he remains in Hel.

object_literal: catches Loki, in salmon form, by the tail
statement: When Loki, as a salmon, tries to leap over the gods' net in the Fránangr falls, Thor catches him by the tail.

object_literal: holds a bowl under the venom dripping onto the bound Loki
statement: With Loki bound by his son's entrails beneath Skaði's serpent, Sigyn holds a bowl to catch the venom; when she empties it, his writhing causes earthquakes.

object_literal: seizes Persephone on the Nysian plain
statement: As Persephone reaches for a narcissus that Earth grew by Zeus's will, the ground opens on the Nysian plain and Hades carries her off in his golden chariot.

object_literal: hears Persephone's cry from her cave
statement: Of all gods and mortals only Hecate in her cave and Helios hear Persephone's cry for help.

object_literal: searches for nine days with blazing torches
statement: Demeter tears off her headband, puts on a dark cloak and searches the earth for nine days with torches, refusing ambrosia, nectar and bathing.

object_literal: tells Demeter that Zeus gave her daughter to Hades
statement: Helios tells Demeter that Zeus gave Persephone to his brother Hades as wife, urging her that Hades is no unworthy son-in-law.

object_literal: disguised as the old woman Doso, becomes a nurse in Eleusis
statement: Angry with Zeus, Demeter leaves Olympus, sits disguised as an old woman named Doso at the Maiden Well in Eleusis, and is taken into King Celeus's house as a nurse.

object_literal: laughs at Iambe's jests and drinks barley, water and pennyroyal
statement: Silent with grief in Celeus's house, Demeter is brought to laugh by Iambe's jests and asks for a drink of barley, water and pennyroyal instead of wine.

object_literal: lays Demophoon in the fire at night to make him immortal
statement: Demeter nurses Demophoon with ambrosia and secretly lays him in the fire at night to make him immortal, until Metaneira sees and cries out.

object_literal: reveals herself and demands a temple at Eleusis
statement: Demeter takes Demophoon from the fire, reveals her divinity, and demands a temple and altar above the Callichorus well where she will teach her rites.

object_literal: causes a year-long famine by hiding the seed
statement: Sitting apart in her new Eleusinian temple, Demeter hides the seed so that nothing grows, bringing a famine that threatens humankind and the gods' offerings.

object_literal: refuses every god's plea until she sees her daughter
statement: Demeter rejects Iris and then all the gods sent by Zeus, vowing not to return to Olympus or let the earth bear fruit until she sees her daughter.

object_literal: secretly gives Persephone a pomegranate seed before releasing her
statement: Obeying Zeus's message brought by Hermes, Hades releases Persephone but secretly gives her a pomegranate seed so that she cannot stay forever with her mother.

object_literal: must spend a third of each year below and return each spring
statement: Reunited with Demeter, Persephone learns that because she ate below she must spend a third of each year under the earth and return each spring.

object_literal: brings Zeus's promise and urges Demeter to end the famine
statement: Zeus sends Rhea to Demeter with his promise of honours and of Persephone's yearly return; Rhea urges her to end the famine.

object_literal: restores the harvest and teaches the Eleusinian mysteries
statement: Demeter makes the fields bear again and teaches her rites and mysteries to Triptolemus, Diocles, Eumolpus and Celeus before returning to Olympus.

object_literal: mingles her waters with Apsû before anything was named
statement: Before heaven and earth were named, Apsû and Tiamat mingle their waters, and from them are born Lahmu and Lahamu, Anshar and Kishar, Anu and Ea.

object_literal: plots to destroy the noisy young gods
statement: Disturbed by the young gods' noise, Apsû plots with his vizier Mummu to destroy them, though Tiamat objects to destroying their own offspring.
Ea puts Apsû to sleep with a pure incantation, takes his crown and aura, kills him and builds his own dwelling upon him.

object_literal: born with four eyes, four ears and fire on his lips
statement: Marduk is born to Ea and Damkina with four eyes and four ears and fiery lips; Anu gives him the four winds, with which he troubles Tiamat.

object_literal: creates eleven monsters and gives Qingu the Tablet of Destinies
statement: Urged to avenge Apsû, Tiamat brings forth eleven monsters, makes Qingu commander of her host and fastens the Tablet of Destinies on his breast.

object_literal: agrees to fight Tiamat if the gods make his word supreme
statement: After Ea and Anu both turn back from Tiamat, Marduk offers to fight her on condition that the gods make his word decree destinies.

object_literal: has his destiny decreed by the gods at a banquet
statement: At a banquet summoned by Anshar, the great gods eat, drink and then assemble to decree Marduk's destiny as their avenger.

object_literal: makes a garment vanish and reappear by his word; proclaimed king
statement: The gods test Marduk's word by having him make a garment vanish and reappear, then proclaim him king and give him sceptre, throne and weapon.
Marduk arms himself with bow, mace, lightning, a net held by the four winds, seven destructive winds, the Flood-weapon and a storm chariot drawn by four poisonous steeds.
In single combat Marduk nets Tiamat, drives the evil wind into her open mouth and shoots an arrow through her belly and heart.

object_literal: is captured and stripped of the Tablet of Destinies
statement: Captured by Marduk after Tiamat's fall, Qingu is stripped of the Tablet of Destinies, which Marduk seals and fastens on his own breast.

object_literal: makes sky and earth from Tiamat's body and orders the stars and months
statement: Marduk splits Tiamat's body like a dried fish, making the sky from one half and the earth from the other, opening the Tigris and Euphrates from her eyes and ordering stars, months and the moon.

object_literal: creates humankind from Qingu's blood to bear the gods' toil
statement: On Marduk's plan Ea creates humankind from the blood of the condemned Qingu, so that humans bear the gods' toil.

object_literal: honoured with Babylon, Esagila and fifty names
statement: The Anunnaki build Babylon and the temple Esagila for Marduk, and the gods proclaim his fifty names.

object_literal: his wife carries Nezha for three years and six months
statement: Li Jing's wife Lady Yin carries her third child for three years and six months and dreams of a Daoist handing her a 'unicorn child'.

object_literal: born from a ball of flesh, wearing the Universe Ring and the Red Armillary Sash
statement: Li Jing cuts open the ball of flesh and a glowing boy springs out wearing a golden ring on his arm and a red silk sash.

object_literal: names the child Nezha and takes him as his disciple
statement: Taiyi Zhenren of the Golden Light Cave names the child Nezha and takes him as his disciple.

object_literal: shakes the Crystal Palace by swishing his sash in the river
statement: At seven, bathing in the Nine Bends River, Nezha swishes his sash in the water and shakes the Dragon King's Crystal Palace.
Nezha kills the patrolling yaksha Li Gen with his ring and then the Dragon King's third son Ao Bing, whose sinew he pulls out.

object_literal: vows to accuse Li Jing and Nezha before the Jade Emperor
statement: Ao Guang comes to Chentang Pass in human form, finds Nezha braiding his son's sinew, and vows to accuse Li Jing and Nezha before the Jade Emperor.

object_literal: beats Ao Guang at the gate of heaven and pockets him as a small snake
statement: Made invisible by Taiyi's charm, Nezha ambushes Ao Guang outside the Gate of Treasured Virtue, tears off his scales and carries him home as a little green snake.

object_literal: kills Lady Shiji's disciple with an arrow from the Universe Bow
statement: Nezha draws the Yellow Emperor's Universe Bow and his arrow kills the Green Cloud boy, disciple of Lady Shiji.

object_literal: burns Lady Shiji back into her stone form with the Nine-Dragon Divine Fire Cover
statement: Taiyi Zhenren traps Lady Shiji under his Nine-Dragon Divine Fire Cover and burns her back into her original form, a stone.

object_literal: returns his flesh and bones to his parents to save them
statement: To free his parents from the four dragon kings, Nezha cuts open his body and returns his flesh and bones to his parents, and dies.

object_literal: smashes Nezha's statue and burns his shrine on Cuiping Mountain
statement: Finding pilgrims at the shrine his wife secretly built for Nezha on Cuiping Mountain, Li Jing smashes the statue and burns the shrine.

object_literal: rebuilds Nezha from lotus and gives him the fire-tipped spear and wind-and-fire wheels
statement: Taiyi Zhenren rebuilds Nezha's body from lotus stems and leaves with an elixir pill and gives him the fire-tipped spear and the wind-and-fire wheels.

object_literal: receives the golden pagoda and the title Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King
statement: Pursued by the reborn Nezha, Li Jing receives the golden pagoda from Randeng Daoren, which forces Nezha to acknowledge him and gives him the title Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King.

object_literal: saw the Deep and built the wall of Uruk
statement: The prologue of the Standard Babylonian epic presents Gilgamesh as the one who saw the Deep, built the wall of Uruk and recorded his labours on a stone tablet.

object_literal: two-thirds god, oppresses the people of Uruk
statement: Two-thirds god and one-third man, Gilgamesh oppresses the young men and women of Uruk until the people cry out to the gods.

object_literal: made by Aruru from clay thrown into the wild
statement: The goddess Aruru pinches off clay and throws it into the wild, making the hairy Enkidu, who lives among the gazelles and frees the trapper's prey.

object_literal: gains human understanding through Shamhat
statement: After six days and seven nights with Shamhat, Enkidu is shunned by the beasts but gains understanding, while Gilgamesh dreams of the companion who is coming.

object_literal: wrestles Gilgamesh at the bridal door and becomes his friend
statement: Civilised with bread and beer among the shepherds, Enkidu bars Gilgamesh from a bridal house in Uruk; after wrestling like bulls, the two become friends.

object_literal: resolves to kill Humbaba to win lasting fame
statement: Seeking lasting fame because human days are numbered, Gilgamesh resolves to kill Humbaba of the Cedar Forest, and Ninsun prays to Shamash for him.

object_literal: interprets Gilgamesh's dreams on the road as favourable
statement: On the road to the Cedar Forest, Enkidu interprets each of Gilgamesh's terrifying dreams as a favourable omen.

object_literal: sends thirteen winds that pin Humbaba
statement: Shamash sends thirteen winds that pin Humbaba in place, allowing Gilgamesh and Enkidu to kill him despite his pleas.

object_literal: proposes marriage to Gilgamesh and is refused
statement: Ishtar proposes marriage to Gilgamesh, who refuses her by recounting the fates of her former lovers, from Dumuzi to the gardener Ishullanu.
With Enkidu holding the Bull of Heaven by its horns, Gilgamesh drives his sword between its nape and horns and kills it.

object_literal: is condemned by the gods, falls sick and dies after twelve days
statement: The gods decree that Enkidu must die for the deaths of Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven; he curses and then blesses Shamhat, dreams of the House of Dust, and dies after twelve days.
Gilgamesh laments Enkidu, veils his face like a bride's, paces like a lioness bereft of her cubs, and commissions a statue of gold and lapis lazuli.

object_literal: walks twelve double-hours of darkness through Mount Mashu
statement: Fearing death, Gilgamesh passes the scorpion-people of Mount Mashu and walks twelve double-hours of darkness to a garden of jewelled trees.

object_literal: crosses the Waters of Death to Uta-napishti
statement: Guided by the alewife Siduri and the boatman Urshanabi, Gilgamesh crosses the Waters of Death with three hundred punting poles and reaches Uta-napishti.

object_literal: survives the Flood and is granted eternal life
statement: Uta-napishti tells how Ea warned him through a reed wall, how he built a boat and survived the six-day Flood, released a dove, a swallow and a raven, and was granted eternal life by Enlil.

object_literal: fails the test of sleep and loses the plant of rejuvenation to a snake
statement: Gilgamesh fails Uta-napishti's test of staying awake, wins the plant 'An Old Man Grows Young' from the deep, loses it to a snake, and returns to the walls of Uruk.

object_literal: abandons seven temples and sets her mind on the netherworld
statement: Inana sets her mind on the great below and abandons heaven, earth, her priestly offices and seven temples in seven cities.

object_literal: adorns herself with seven divine powers as regalia
statement: Inana takes up the seven divine powers as regalia: crown, wig, lapis beads, egg-shaped beads, pala dress, eye-paint and pectoral, gold ring and measuring rod and line.

object_literal: is instructed to lament and seek help from Enlil, Nanna and Enki
statement: Inana instructs Ninšubur to lament for her and to seek help from Enlil, then Nanna, then Enki if she does not return.

object_literal: orders the seven gates bolted and Inana stripped as she enters
statement: Told that Inana has come for her husband's funeral rites, Ereškigala orders the seven gates bolted and Inana stripped of her regalia as she enters.

object_literal: is stripped of one item of regalia at each of the seven gates
statement: At each of the seven gates one of Inana's regalia is removed, and each time she is told to be satisfied, for a divine power of the netherworld has been fulfilled.

object_literal: turns Inana into a corpse with the look of death
statement: When Inana sits on her throne, Ereškigala fixes her with the look of death, and the Anuna judges condemn her; Inana becomes a corpse hung on a hook.

object_literal: refuses to help Inana, who craved the netherworld's powers
statement: When Ninšubur pleads for Inana after three days and nights, Enlil angrily refuses, saying whoever craves the netherworld's powers must remain there; Nanna also refuses.

object_literal: creates two rescuers from the dirt under his fingernails
statement: Enki creates the kur-ĝara and the gala-tura from the dirt under his fingernails and sends them with the plant and water of life to rescue Inana.

object_literal: is revived with the plant and water of life
statement: Enki's creatures win Ereškigala's gratitude, refuse her gifts, take Inana's corpse from the hook and revive her with the plant and water of life.

object_literal: must provide a substitute and is escorted by the galla demons
statement: The Anuna let Inana ascend only if she provides a substitute, and the galla demons who know no food, drink or gifts go up with her.

object_literal: spares Ninšubur, Šara and Lulal because they mourned for her
statement: Inana refuses to hand Ninšubur, Šara or Lulal to the demons because each mourned for her in dirty garments.

object_literal: is handed over as Inana's substitute and flees with snake's hands and feet
statement: Found enthroned and unmourning, Dumuzid is given to the demons by Inana; Utu changes his hands and feet into snake's so he can escape, and the broken ending divides the year between him and his sister.

object_literal: divides the realms among his three noble children
statement: Izanagi gives Amaterasu his jewel necklace and the Plain of High Heaven, Tsukuyomi the dominion of night and Susanoo the plain of the sea.

object_literal: weeps until mountains wither and is expelled
statement: Susanoo weeps until his beard grows long, the mountains wither and the seas dry, saying he wants to go to his mother's land; Izanagi expels him.

object_literal: arms herself to meet Susanoo
statement: Fearing that Susanoo comes to seize her land, Amaterasu binds her hair like a man, arms herself with jewels, quivers and bow and stamps the earth as she waits for him.

object_literal: swears the oath of child-bearing with Susanoo
statement: Across the Tranquil River of Heaven Amaterasu crunches Susanoo's sabre and blows out three goddesses, and Susanoo crunches her jewels and blows out five male deities.

object_literal: claims victory in the oath
statement: Amaterasu assigns the five male deities to herself and the three goddesses to Susanoo, who claims that his gentle daughters prove his pure heart and that he has won.

object_literal: ravages the Plain of High Heaven
statement: Susanoo breaks Amaterasu's rice-field ridges, defiles her hall and flings a backward-flayed piebald horse into her weaving hall, causing a weaving maiden's death.
Terrified, Amaterasu shuts herself in the Heavenly Rock-Dwelling, so that Heaven and the Central Land of Reed-Plains fall into continual night and calamities arise.

object_literal: devises the plan to draw Amaterasu out
statement: The eight hundred myriad deities assemble in the bed of the Tranquil River of Heaven and have Omoikane devise a plan: singing birds, a mirror, a string of jewels and divination by a stag's shoulder-blade.

object_literal: hides beside the door of the Rock-Dwelling
statement: The deities hang jewels, a mirror and cloth offerings on a sakaki tree from Mount Kagu; Futotama holds it, Ame-no-Koyane recites a liturgy and Tajikarao hides beside the door.

object_literal: dances before the Rock-Dwelling until the deities laugh
statement: Ame-no-Uzume stamps on an upturned tub before the Rock-Dwelling, becomes divinely possessed and bares herself, so that the Plain of High Heaven shakes with the laughter of the deities.
When Amaterasu opens the door a crack and is shown the mirror, Ame-no-Tajikarao draws her out by the hand and Futotama stretches a rope behind her, and light returns.
Expelled from Heaven, Susanoo kills the food goddess Ōgetsuhime, and silkworms, rice, millet, beans and barley grow from her body; Kami-musubi takes them as seeds.

object_literal: eight heads and eight tails, spanning eight valleys and eight hills
statement: Ashinazuchi tells Susanoo that the eight-forked serpent of Koshi, with eight heads and eight tails, eyes like red winter-cherries and a body spanning eight valleys and hills, has devoured seven of his eight daughters.
Susanoo makes the eight-forked serpent drunk with eight vats of liquor, cuts it to pieces, finds a great sword in its middle tail and presents it to Amaterasu.

object_literal: builds the palace of Suga and sings of the eightfold fence
statement: Susanoo builds his palace at Suga in Izumo, saying his heart is refreshed, sings the song of the eightfold fence as clouds rise, and makes Ashinazuchi master of the palace.

object_literal: wins five epagomenal days from the Moon
statement: In Plutarch's account Hermes (Thoth) wins a seventieth part of each day's light from the Moon at draughts and composes the five epagomenal days, on which Rhea (Nut) can give birth.
tradition_scope: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek reception of the Osiris myth)

object_literal: born on the first epagomenal day
statement: Plutarch lists the births on the five added days: Osiris, Arueris (the elder Horus), Typhon who bursts through his mother's side, Isis and Nephthys.
tradition_scope: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek reception of the Osiris myth)

object_literal: teaches cultivation, laws and worship
statement: Plutarch says Osiris as king taught the Egyptians cultivation, laws and worship, then civilised the world by persuasion and music rather than weapons.
tradition_scope: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek reception of the Osiris myth)

object_literal: traps Osiris in a sealed chest
statement: In Plutarch's account Typhon (Seth) and seventy-two conspirators trap Osiris in a chest made to his measure, seal it with nails and molten lead and send it to the sea by the Tanitic mouth.
tradition_scope: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek reception of the Osiris myth)

statement: Plutarch says that on hearing of the murder Isis cut a lock of her hair at Coptos, put on mourning and searched everywhere, learning the river mouth from children at play.
tradition_scope: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek reception of the Osiris myth)

object_literal: rears the abandoned child Anubis
statement: In Plutarch's account Isis, guided by dogs, finds and rears the child Nephthys abandoned for fear of Typhon; he becomes her guardian Anubis.
tradition_scope: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek reception of the Osiris myth)

object_literal: seeks the coffin enclosed in a pillar at Byblos
statement: Plutarch tells that the chest lodged in a heather tree at Byblos, which grew around it; the king made the trunk a pillar of his palace, and Isis came to Byblos and sat weeping by a spring.
tradition_scope: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek reception of the Osiris myth)

object_literal: takes the coffin from the pillar at Byblos
statement: Plutarch says Isis, as nurse to the Byblian prince, burned away his mortality by night until the queen's cry broke the rite; then she revealed herself and took the coffin from the pillar.
tradition_scope: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek reception of the Osiris myth)

statement: Plutarch describes Isis opening the chest in a solitary place, laying her face on Osiris's face and weeping; the Byblian boy who sees her dies at her look.
tradition_scope: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek reception of the Osiris myth)

object_literal: tears the body into fourteen parts
statement: In Plutarch's account Typhon (Seth), hunting by moonlight, finds the body of Osiris, tears it into fourteen parts and scatters them; Isis recovers them in a papyrus boat.
tradition_scope: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek reception of the Osiris myth)

object_literal: prevails over Typhon after many days of battle
statement: Plutarch says Osiris returned from the other world to train Horus, who answers that the noblest deed is to avenge one's parents, and who prevails over Typhon after many days of battle.
tradition_scope: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek reception of the Osiris myth)

object_literal: releases the captured Typhon
statement: Plutarch says Isis released the captured Typhon, Horus tore the diadem from her head, the gods with Hermes' help judged Horus legitimate, and the tomb of Osiris is placed on an inaccessible island near Philae.
tradition_scope: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek reception of the Osiris myth)

object_literal: opens with the grief that became the first śloka
statement: The opening cantos tell how Vālmīki's grief at a hunter killing a curlew became the first śloka and how Brahmā commanded him to sing the story of Rāma in that metre.

object_literal: agrees to be born as the sons of Daśaratha to slay Rāvaṇa
statement: At the gods' plea against Rāvaṇa, whose boon protected him from gods and demons but not men, Vishnu agrees to be born as the four sons of Daśaratha, who receives the divine rice-milk from his sacrificial fire.

object_literal: guards Viśvāmitra's sacrifice and slays Tāṭakā
statement: Lent to Viśvāmitra to guard his sacrifice, Rāma slays the rākṣasī Tāṭakā at the sage's urging, receives the divine weapons and drives off Mārīca and Subāhu.
At Mithilā Rāma lifts, strings and breaks the bow of Śiva that no king could lift, and Janaka gives him Sītā, the daughter found in a furrow.

object_literal: is bound by two boons to exile Rāma
statement: Persuaded by her maid Mantharā, Kaikeyī claims Daśaratha's two old boons: Bharata's consecration and Rāma's exile to the forest for fourteen years.

object_literal: insists on following Rāma into exile
statement: When Rāma accepts exile without a change of face, Sītā insists that a wife shares her husband's lot and follows him into the forest with Lakṣmaṇa, all three in bark garments.

object_literal: dies of grief, fulfilling an old curse
statement: After Rāma leaves, Daśaratha tells Kausalyā how in youth he shot a young ascetic by mistake and was cursed by the boy's blind father to die grieving for a son, and dies at midnight.

object_literal: rules Ayodhyā in the name of Rāma's sandals
statement: Refusing the throne, Bharata seeks Rāma at Citrakūṭa; when Rāma will not break their father's word, Bharata takes his sandals, sets them on the throne and rules from Nandigrāma as their servant.

object_literal: cuts off Śūrpaṇakhā's nose and ears
statement: At Pañcavaṭī, when the rākṣasī Śūrpaṇakhā, rebuffed by both brothers, attacks Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa cuts off her nose and ears at Rāma's command, and Rāma then destroys the army of Khara and Dūṣaṇa alone.

object_literal: sends Mārīca as a golden deer to lure Rāma away
statement: Rāvaṇa forces Mārīca to take the form of a golden deer, which lures Rāma away; dying, Mārīca cries out in Rāma's voice so that Sītā sends Lakṣmaṇa after him.
Disguised as an ascetic, Rāvaṇa seizes Sītā and carries her to Laṅkā, cutting down the vulture-king Jaṭāyu who tries to stop him, while Sītā drops her ornaments to five monkeys.

object_literal: performs funeral rites for the vulture Jaṭāyu
statement: Finding the hut empty, Rāma learns from the dying Jaṭāyu that Rāvaṇa took Sītā south, cremates the vulture as a father, and is directed by Kabandha to seek Sugrīva.

object_literal: allies with Sugrīva and shoots Vālin from concealment
statement: Rāma allies with Sugrīva through Hanumān, shoots Vālin from concealment and answers his reproach, makes Sugrīva king and gives his ring to Hanumān for the southern search.

object_literal: leaps the hundred-league sea to Laṅkā
statement: Told by Sampāti that Sītā is in Laṅkā and reminded by Jāmbavān of his strength, Hanumān leaps the hundred-league sea from Mount Mahendra, passing Maināka, Surasā and Siṃhikā.
Hanumān finds Sītā in the aśoka grove after Rāvaṇa threatens her, gives her Rāma's ring, and receives her crest-jewel when she declines to be carried away by him.
Captured by Indrajit and sentenced by Rāvaṇa, Hanumān has his tail set alight, feels no heat through Sītā's prayer, and burns Laṅkā before leaping back with her crest-jewel.

object_literal: crosses to Laṅkā by the bridge built by Nala
statement: Rāma grants refuge to Vibhīṣaṇa and, after the Ocean rises at his threatened arrow, has Nala build a bridge to Laṅkā in five days and lays siege to the city.

object_literal: slays Indrajit
statement: In the war before Laṅkā Garuḍa frees the brothers from Indrajit's serpent-arrows, Rāma slays Kumbhakarṇa, Hanumān brings the mountain of herbs, and Lakṣmaṇa slays Indrajit.
In single combat, with Indra's chariot driven by Mātali, Rāma strikes off Rāvaṇa's regrowing heads and finally kills him with the weapon of Brahmā, then tells Vibhīṣaṇa that enmity ends with death.

object_literal: passes through fire and is restored to Rāma
statement: After Rāma's harsh public words Sītā enters a pyre and Agni returns her unharmed and declares her pure; the gods proclaim Rāma to be Nārāyaṇa, and Rāma returns to Ayodhyā to be crowned.

object_literal: the Muses give Hesiod a laurel staff and the gift of song
statement: Hesiod says the Muses gave him a laurel staff and a divine voice beneath Helicon and asks them to tell how the gods first came to be.

object_literal: comes to be first of all
statement: In the Theogony Chaos comes to be first, followed by Earth, Tartarus and Eros; Earth then bears starry Heaven, the hills and the sea.

object_literal: bears the Titans, the Cyclopes and the Hundred-Handers
statement: Earth and Heaven produce the twelve Titans, youngest of them Cronus, together with the three Cyclopes and the three Hundred-Handers.

object_literal: castrates Ouranos with Earth's sickle
statement: With a sickle of adamant made by Earth, Cronus ambushes Heaven and castrates him; from the blood come the Erinyes, the Giants and the Meliai.

object_literal: born from the sea-foam and comes ashore at Cyprus
statement: Aphrodite grows from the foam around Heaven's severed members, comes ashore at Cythera and Cyprus, and is attended by Eros and Desire.

object_literal: bears Doom, Death, Sleep, the Fates and Strife without a partner
statement: Night, alone, bears Doom, Death, Sleep, Dreams, the Fates, Nemesis and Strife, while the line of Sea produces Nereus, the Gorgons, Echidna and her monstrous brood.

object_literal: given a share of honour in earth, sea and heaven by Zeus
statement: Zeus honours Hecate above all, granting her a share of earth, sea and starry heaven; she gives success to those she favours.

object_literal: swallows his children as they are born
statement: Warned that a son will overthrow him, Cronus swallows each child Rhea bears: Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades and Poseidon.

object_literal: saves Zeus by giving Cronus a swaddled stone
statement: Rhea bears Zeus secretly in Crete and gives Cronus a stone in swaddling clothes to swallow; Cronus later vomits up the stone and his children.

object_literal: tricks Zeus at Mecone and steals fire in a fennel stalk
statement: At Mecone Prometheus tricks Zeus over the sacrifice and then steals fire in a fennel stalk; Zeus chains him and sends an eagle to eat his liver until Heracles frees him.

object_literal: moulds the first woman from earth at Zeus's will
statement: At Zeus's will Hephaestus moulds the first woman from earth and Athena adorns her, as Zeus's answer to the theft of fire.

object_literal: frees the Hundred-Handers and wins their alliance
statement: After ten years of indecisive war, Zeus follows Earth's advice, brings the Hundred-Handers up to the light and wins their alliance against the Titans.

object_literal: defeats the Titans with thunderbolts and the Hundred-Handers' rocks
statement: Zeus unleashes his thunderbolts while the Hundred-Handers hurl three hundred rocks at a time, and the Titans are cast down beneath the earth in chains.

object_literal: as far below the earth as heaven is above it; an anvil falls nine days to reach it
statement: Hesiod places Tartarus as far below the earth as heaven is above, a bronze anvil falling nine days to reach it, with the houses of Night, Sleep, Death, Hades and Styx nearby.
Zeus strikes the hundred-headed Typhoeus with lightning, burns his heads and hurls him into Tartarus.

object_literal: chosen king of the gods; swallows Metis and bears Athena from his head
statement: The gods ask Zeus to reign on Earth's advice; he swallows Metis to forestall a son who would overthrow him, bears Athena from his head and takes his later wives.

object_literal: raises his goats from their bones and takes Þjálfi and Röskva as servants
statement: Thor raises his slaughtered goats with Mjöllnir; finding one lame because Þjálfi split its bone, he takes Þjálfi and Röskva as servants.

object_literal: shelters for a night in the giant Skrýmir's glove
statement: Travelling into Jötunheimr, Thor and his companions spend a night in what proves to be the glove of the giant Skrýmir.

object_literal: strikes the sleeping Skrýmir three times without harming him
statement: Thor cannot untie Skrýmir's provision bag and strikes the sleeping giant three times with his hammer, but the giant only asks whether a leaf, an acorn or bird droppings fell on him.

object_literal: mocks Thor and demands a contest of skills
statement: Útgarða-Loki mocks Thor as a 'little lad' and demands that each visitor prove some skill before he may stay.

object_literal: loses an eating contest to Logi
statement: Loki loses an eating contest to Logi, who devours the meat, the bones and the trough itself.

object_literal: loses three races to Hugi
statement: Þjálfi races Hugi three times and loses each heat by a wider margin.

object_literal: fails to empty the drinking horn in three draughts
statement: Thor drinks three mighty draughts from Útgarða-Loki's penalty horn but cannot empty it.

object_literal: lifts only one paw of the grey cat
statement: Straining his utmost, Thor manages to lift only one paw of Útgarða-Loki's grey cat from the floor.

object_literal: is forced to one knee by the old woman Elli
statement: Thor wrestles Útgarða-Loki's old nurse Elli and is forced down onto one knee.

object_literal: reveals that the contests were illusions: fire, thought, the sea, the Serpent and old age
statement: Útgarða-Loki reveals he was Skrýmir and that Thor's opponents were wildfire, thought, the sea, the Midgard Serpent and old age.

object_literal: raises his hammer as Útgarða-Loki and his castle vanish
statement: When Thor raises his hammer, Útgarða-Loki and his stronghold vanish, leaving only open plains; Thor resolves to meet the Midgard Serpent again.

object_literal: hooks the Midgard Serpent while fishing with Hymir
statement: Fishing with the giant Hymir using an ox head for bait, Thor hooks the Midgard Serpent and hauls it to the boat before Hymir cuts the line.

object_literal: born from a stone egg on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit
statement: A stone on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit splits into a stone egg that becomes a monkey whose eyes flash light to heaven.

object_literal: leaps through the waterfall and becomes Handsome Monkey King
statement: The stone monkey leaps through the waterfall, finds the Water Curtain Cave and is acclaimed Handsome Monkey King.

object_literal: sails away on a raft to seek the secret of long life
statement: Grieving that the King of the Dead will one day claim him, the Monkey King sails alone across the sea to seek immortality.

object_literal: names the monkey Sun Wukong
statement: Patriarch Subodhi receives the monkey at the Cave of the Slanting Moon and Three Stars and names him Sun Wukong.

object_literal: learns the seventy-two transformations and the somersault cloud
statement: Understanding the patriarch's three blows as a riddle, Wukong is secretly taught long life, the seventy-two transformations and the somersault cloud.

object_literal: expels Wukong for showing off and forbids him to name his teacher
statement: After Wukong shows off by becoming a pine tree, the patriarch expels him and forbids him ever to name his teacher.

object_literal: yields the ocean-fixing iron, the Compliant Golden-Hooped Rod
statement: Ao Guang, Dragon King of the Eastern Sea, lets Sun Wukong take the 13,500-pound iron that becomes the Compliant Golden-Hooped Rod.

object_literal: strikes the monkeys' names from the Register of Life and Death
statement: Dragged to the underworld in a dream, Wukong strikes his own name and those of all monkeys from the Register of Life and Death.

object_literal: appoints Wukong Keeper of the Heavenly Horses
statement: On Venus's advice the Jade Emperor summons Wukong to heaven and appoints him Keeper of the Heavenly Horses, a post without rank.

object_literal: grants the empty title Great Sage Equal to Heaven
statement: After Heavenly King Li and Nezha fail to capture him, the Jade Emperor grants Wukong the empty title Great Sage Equal to Heaven and builds him a mansion.

object_literal: eats the immortal peaches he was set to guard
statement: Put in charge of the Garden of Immortal Peaches, Wukong secretly eats the ripest peaches and learns he is not invited to the Peach Banquet.

object_literal: steals the banquet wine and Laozi's elixir, then defeats heaven's army
statement: Wukong drinks the banquet wine, eats Laozi's elixir pills and holds off a hundred thousand heavenly soldiers at his mountain.

object_literal: matches the Great Sage's transformations and captures him
statement: Erlang matches every transformation of the Great Sage until Laozi's Diamond Snare and Erlang's hound bring him down.

object_literal: refines the Great Sage in the Eight Trigrams furnace for forty-nine days
statement: Laozi refines the captured Great Sage in his Eight Trigrams furnace for forty-nine days; he emerges with fiery golden eyes and kicks the furnace over.

object_literal: wagers that the Great Sage cannot leave his palm
statement: Rulai wagers that the Great Sage cannot somersault out of his right palm; the monkey leaps and reaches five pink pillars he takes for the edge of heaven.

object_literal: pins the Great Sage under the Mountain of Five Elements
statement: Rulai reveals the Great Sage's graffiti on his own finger and turns his hand into the Mountain of Five Elements, pinning the monkey beneath it.

object_literal: disguises Odysseus as an old beggar on his return to Ithaca
statement: When the Phaeacians leave the sleeping Odysseus in Ithaca, Athena reveals herself, praises his cunning, helps him hide his treasure and disguises him as an old beggar.

The swineherd Eumaeus shelters the disguised Odysseus, refuses to believe his oath that Odysseus will return, gives him his own cloak and tells how he was kidnapped as a king's son and sold to Laertes.

object_literal: evades the suitors' ambush on his return from Sparta
statement: Warned by Athena of the suitors' ambush in the strait, Telemachus leaves Sparta, takes the fugitive seer Theoclymenus aboard at Pylos, avoids the ambush by sailing at night and lands secretly on Ithaca.
In the swineherd's hut Athena restores Odysseus's form and he reveals himself to Telemachus; father and son weep together and plan the suitors' death in secrecy.

object_literal: is recognised by his old dog Argos at the palace door
statement: Entering Ithaca as a beggar, Odysseus is kicked by Melanthius and restrains himself; at the palace door his old dog Argos recognises his voice, wags his tail and dies after twenty years.
In his own hall the beggar Odysseus is struck with a footstool by Antinous, breaks the jaw of the beggar Irus in a boxing match staged by the suitors, and vainly warns the kindly Amphinomus to leave.
Washing the disguised Odysseus's feet, his old nurse Eurycleia recognises the boar-tusk scar from his youth on Parnassus; he silences her while Athena keeps Penelope from noticing.

object_literal: announces the contest of the bow and the twelve axes
statement: Penelope tells the disguised Odysseus her dream of an eagle killing twenty geese, distinguishes the gates of horn and ivory, and announces a contest of Odysseus's bow and twelve axes; next day omens of the suitors' doom multiply.

object_literal: is strung by Odysseus, who shoots through the twelve axes
statement: No suitor can string the bow Iphitus gave Odysseus; having revealed himself to Eumaeus and Philoetius, Odysseus strings it like a lyre and shoots through all twelve axes.

object_literal: takes vengeance on the suitors from the threshold of his hall
statement: From the threshold of his hall Odysseus kills Antinous with his first arrow, refuses Eurymachus's offer of compensation and, with Telemachus, the two loyal herdsmen and Athena's aegis, defeats the suitors, sparing the bard Phemius and the herald Medon.

object_literal: forbids exulting over the dead and purifies his house
statement: After the killing of the suitors Odysseus forbids Eurycleia to exult over the dead, punishes the twelve disloyal maids and Melanthius, and purifies the house with sulphur and fire.
Penelope tests the returned Odysseus by ordering his bed moved; his angry account of the bed built on a living olive trunk, a secret only they know, convinces her and they are reunited.

As Hermes leads the suitors' souls to Hades, Odysseus finds his aged father Laertes working in his orchard; after testing him with a tale, he proves his identity by his scar and the trees Laertes once gave him.

object_literal: ends the feud in Ithaca and establishes peace
statement: When the suitors' kin led by Eupeithes attack Odysseus at Laertes's farm, Athena with Zeus's sanction and thunderbolt stops the fighting and, in the guise of Mentor, establishes lasting peace in Ithaca.

object_literal: persuades Zeus to let Odysseus return home
statement: In the Odyssey's opening council, while Poseidon is away, Athena persuades Zeus to let Odysseus, held by Calypso, return home, and proposes to send Hermes to Calypso and to rouse Telemachus herself.

object_literal: is roused by Athena disguised as Mentes
statement: Athena, disguised as Mentes, tells Telemachus that Odysseus lives and urges him to confront the suitors and seek news of his father at Pylos and Sparta; Telemachus asserts himself as master of the house.

object_literal: weaves Laertes' shroud by day and unpicks it by night
statement: At the Ithacan assembly Antinous reveals how Penelope put off the suitors for three years by weaving a shroud for Laertes by day and unpicking it by night; Telemachus refuses to send her away and secretly sails with Athena's help.

object_literal: learns at Sparta that Odysseus is held by Calypso
statement: Telemachus hears from Nestor at Pylos of the Greeks' homecomings and from Menelaus at Sparta that Proteus told him Odysseus lives, held by Calypso, while the suitors lay an ambush for his return.
Ordered by Zeus through Hermes, Calypso releases Odysseus after seven years, and Odysseus tells her that though Penelope cannot match a goddess's beauty, he longs every day for home.
Seeing Odysseus on his raft within sight of the Phaeacians' land, Poseidon wrecks it with a storm; aided by Ino's veil and a river god, Odysseus swims ashore after two days and nights.

object_literal: supplicates the princess Nausicaa
statement: Shipwrecked on the Phaeacians' shore, Odysseus is woken by Nausicaa and her maids at play; he supplicates her with courteous words, and she gives him clothes and directs him to her mother at the palace.

object_literal: reveals his name at the Phaeacian court
statement: At the Phaeacian court Odysseus wins the discus throw, weeps when the bard Demodocus sings of the wooden horse, and at King Alcinous's question reveals his name and begins to tell his wanderings.

object_literal: drags his men away from the Lotus-eaters
statement: Odysseus tells how after a costly raid on the Cicones his scouts ate the lotus in the land of the Lotus-eaters and forgot their homecoming, and how he dragged them weeping back to the ships.
The Cyclops Polyphemus seals Odysseus and his men in his cave with a stone, scorns Zeus as protector of guests and eats two of the men at night and two more in the morning.
Telling Polyphemus his name is 'Nobody', Odysseus makes him drunk and blinds his single eye with a heated stake, so that the other Cyclopes leave when he cries that 'Nobody' is killing him.

Odysseus and his men escape the blind Polyphemus clinging under his rams; when Odysseus boastfully shouts his true name, the Cyclops prays to Poseidon that Odysseus reach home late, alone and to find trouble there.

object_literal: loses his fleet after the bag of winds is opened
statement: Odysseus tells how his men opened Aeolus's bag of winds within sight of Ithaca and were blown back, and how the man-eating Laestrygonians destroyed every ship but his own.

Circe turns Odysseus's men into swine; protected by the herb moly from Hermes, Odysseus makes her swear not to harm him and restore them, stays a year, and is told he must consult Tiresias in the house of Hades.

object_literal: consults Tiresias among the dead
statement: At the edge of the world Odysseus calls up the dead with blood; Tiresias prophesies his late and lonely return and his revenge on the suitors, his mother's shade slips from his embrace, and Achilles says he would rather be a hired hand on earth than king among the dead.
Following Circe's advice, Odysseus seals his crew's ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast, so that he hears the Sirens' song of all knowledge without being able to turn to them.
Passing between Scylla and Charybdis as Circe advised, Odysseus loses six of his strongest men to the six heads of Scylla while the crew watches Charybdis swallow the sea.

object_literal: has Zeus destroy Odysseus's ship for the slaughter of his cattle
statement: When Odysseus's starving men slaughter the cattle of the Sun on Thrinacia, Helios demands vengeance and Zeus's thunderbolt destroys the ship; Odysseus alone survives, escapes Charybdis and drifts to Calypso's island.

object_literal: vows to protect the hermits and buries Virādha
statement: Entering the Daṇḍaka forest, Rāma promises the hermits protection from the rākṣasas, and with Lakṣmaṇa overcomes and buries the weapon-proof rākṣasa Virādha, who seized Sītā and turns out to be a cursed gandharva.

object_literal: warns Rāma against violence without cause
statement: Sītā warns Rāma against violence without cause, telling of a hermit corrupted by keeping a sword, and Rāma answers that a warrior must protect those who seek his help and keep his promise to the sages.

object_literal: befriends Rāma and offers to guard Sītā
statement: After ten years among the hermits and gifts of weapons from Agastya, Rāma meets the vulture-king Jaṭāyu, friend of Daśaratha, who offers to guard Sītā, and settles at Pañcavaṭī on the Godāvarī.
When Śūrpaṇakhā, rebuffed in jest by both brothers, rushes to devour Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa cuts off her nose and ears at Rāma's command.

object_literal: alone destroys Khara's fourteen thousand
statement: With Lakṣmaṇa guarding Sītā in a cave, Rāma alone destroys Khara's army of fourteen thousand rākṣasas, Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras, and kills Khara with Agastya's arrow.
Told of Khara's defeat and berated by Śūrpaṇakhā, who praises Sītā's beauty before his court, Rāvaṇa resolves to abduct Sītā.

object_literal: warns Rāvaṇa and is forced to obey
statement: Mārīca, who has lived in terror of Rāma since his boyhood arrow, warns Rāvaṇa against abducting Sītā, but agrees to become the golden deer when Rāvaṇa threatens to kill him.

object_literal: becomes a jewelled golden deer
statement: Mārīca takes the form of a jewelled golden deer; Sītā begs Rāma to catch it despite Lakṣmaṇa's warning, and Rāma leaves Lakṣmaṇa to guard her while he pursues it.
When the dying Mārīca cries out in Rāma's voice, Sītā accuses Lakṣmaṇa of wanting Rāma dead in order to possess her, until he leaves to search for Rāma, calling the forest gods to witness.

object_literal: woos Sītā in the guise of an ascetic
statement: Disguised as a wandering brahmin, Rāvaṇa is welcomed by Sītā as a guest, then reveals himself and asks her to be his queen in Laṅkā; she scorns him as a jackal coveting a lioness.
The aged vulture-king Jaṭāyu fights Rāvaṇa in the sky to save Sītā, wrecking his chariot and breaking his bow, until Rāvaṇa cuts off his wings and feet.
In Laṅkā Rāvaṇa shows Sītā his palace and offers to be her slave; when she refuses, speaking across a blade of grass, he gives her twelve months and confines her in the aśoka grove.
Finding the hut empty, Rāma is restrained by Lakṣmaṇa from destroying the worlds in grief, learns from the dying Jaṭāyu that Rāvaṇa took Sītā south and cremates him as a father.

object_literal: is directed by Kabandha toward Sugrīva
statement: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa cut off the arms of the headless Kabandha, whose cremation releases a celestial who directs them to Sugrīva; the aged ascetic Śabarī welcomes Rāma and rises to heaven.

object_literal: resolves to consecrate Rāma as heir
statement: Aging and seeing ill omens, Daśaratha proposes Rāma as heir to an assembly that acclaims him, and orders the consecration for the next day while Bharata is away.

object_literal: is persuaded to claim her two old boons
statement: Mantharā persuades Kaikeyī that Rāma's consecration will ruin her and Bharata, and reminds her of the two boons Daśaratha promised when she saved him in the war against Śambara.

object_literal: claims Bharata's consecration and Rāma's exile
statement: Lying in the chamber of wrath, Kaikeyī makes Daśaratha swear by Rāma and claims her two boons: Bharata's consecration and Rāma's exile to the Daṇḍaka forest for fourteen years.

object_literal: begs Kaikeyī all night in vain
statement: Through the night Daśaratha begs Kaikeyī to withdraw her demand, but she invokes his duty to keep his word, and at dawn sends Sumantra to summon Rāma.

object_literal: accepts exile without a change of face
statement: Told by Kaikeyī of the two boons, Rāma accepts exile without a change of face, saying he would give up kingdom and life for his father's word, and leaves to take leave of his mother.

object_literal: offers to seize the throne for Rāma and is calmed
statement: When Kausalyā collapses at the news and Lakṣmaṇa offers to seize the throne by force, Rāma calms his brother, attributing Kaikeyī's demand to fate, and receives his mother's blessing.

object_literal: insists on sharing Rāma's exile
statement: Told to stay in Ayodhyā, Sītā answers that a wife shares her husband's lot, that the forest with Rāma is better than heaven, and threatens to die if left behind, until Rāma agrees to take her.

object_literal: follows Rāma into exile in bark garments
statement: Lakṣmaṇa insists on following Rāma; the three give away their wealth and put on the bark garments Kaikeyī brings, while Vasiṣṭha protests that Sītā was never sentenced to wear them.

object_literal: leaves Ayodhyā and crosses the Ganges
statement: Rāma leaves Ayodhyā with the city weeping behind him, slips away from the citizens at the Tamasā, is welcomed by the Niṣāda chief Guha, mats his hair and crosses the Ganges while Sītā prays to Gaṅgā.

object_literal: settles on Mount Citrakūṭa
statement: On the sage Bharadvāja's advice Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa cross the Yamunā and settle in a leaf hut on Mount Citrakūṭa by the Mandākinī.

object_literal: dies of grief, fulfilling an old curse
statement: On the sixth night after Rāma's departure Daśaratha tells Kausalyā how in youth he killed a young ascetic by mistake and was cursed by the blind father to die grieving for a son, and dies calling Rāma's name.

object_literal: rebukes Kaikeyī and refuses the throne
statement: Returning to find his father dead and Rāma exiled for his sake, Bharata rebukes Kaikeyī, stops Śatrughna from killing Mantharā, swears his innocence to Kausalyā and performs the funeral.

object_literal: leads the army to bring Rāma back
statement: Bharata leads the court and army toward the forest to bring Rāma back; Guha and Bharadvāja first suspect him and then honour him, Bharadvāja conjuring a marvellous feast for the army.
When Bharata's army approaches Citrakūṭa, Rāma rebukes Lakṣmaṇa's suspicion; Bharata falls at Rāma's feet and tells him their father has died, and Rāma offers ingudī pulp to Daśaratha's spirit.

object_literal: rejects Jābāli's argument and keeps his father's word
statement: At Citrakūṭa Rāma refuses Bharata's plea to return and sharply rejects the brahmin Jābāli's materialist argument that a dead father's promise does not bind, holding that truth is the root of dharma.

object_literal: rules Ayodhyā in the name of Rāma's sandals
statement: Unable to move Rāma, Bharata takes his gold-adorned sandals, sets them on the throne and rules from Nandigrāma as an ascetic for fourteen years; Rāma moves south past the hermitage of Atri and Anasūyā into the Daṇḍaka forest.

object_literal: begins with the first śloka born of grief
statement: In the opening of Book I Nārada tells Vālmīki of Rāma; Vālmīki's pity for a curlew shot by a hunter becomes the first śloka, and Brahmā commands him to sing the whole story in that metre.

object_literal: is first sung by Kuśa and Lava before Rāma
statement: Book I tells how Vālmīki taught the poem to the twins Kuśa and Lava, who sang it before sages and then before Rāma himself in Ayodhyā.

object_literal: rules Ayodhyā but has no son
statement: Book I describes Ayodhyā under King Daśaratha, who rules well but has no son and resolves on the horse sacrifice, recalling a prophecy about the sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.

object_literal: brings the sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga to Ayodhyā
statement: Book I tells how the forest-bred sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, lured to drought-stricken Aṅga by courtesans, brought rain and married Śāntā, and how Daśaratha brought him to Ayodhyā to lead his sacrifice.

object_literal: agrees to be born as Daśaratha's four sons
statement: During Daśaratha's sacrifice the gods complain of Rāvaṇa, whom only a man can kill; Vishnu agrees to be born as Daśaratha's four sons, and the gods beget vānaras such as Hanumān, Vālin and Sugrīva to help him.
A being rising from the sacrificial fire gives Daśaratha heavenly rice-milk for his queens, and Kausalyā bears Rāma, Kaikeyī Bharata, and Sumitrā the twins Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna.
Viśvāmitra asks Daśaratha for the young Rāma to guard his sacrifice from Mārīca and Subāhu; the king refuses until Vasiṣṭha persuades him to keep his word.

object_literal: slays the rākṣasī Tāṭakā
statement: On the road with Viśvāmitra Rāma receives the spells Balā and Atibalā and, reluctant to kill a woman until the sage urges him, slays the rākṣasī Tāṭakā.

object_literal: receives the divine weapons and protects the sacrifice
statement: Viśvāmitra gives Rāma the divine weapons; at Siddhāśrama Rāma hurls Mārīca a hundred leagues into the sea, kills Subāhu and completes the sage's sacrifice.

object_literal: descends from heaven through Śiva's hair
statement: Viśvāmitra tells Rāma how Bhagīratha's austerities brought the Ganges down from heaven, how Śiva caught her proud fall in his hair, and how her waters raised Sagara's sixty thousand sons to heaven.

object_literal: rises from king to brahmin sage through austerities
statement: Śatānanda tells how Viśvāmitra, a king humbled by Vasiṣṭha over the wish-cow Śabalā, rose through thousands of years of austerities, despite Menakā and his own anger, to be acknowledged a brahmin sage.

object_literal: is released from Gautama's curse when Rāma enters the hermitage
statement: Book I tells how Ahalyā, cursed by her husband Gautama after Indra deceived her in Gautama's form, lived unseen in the deserted hermitage until Rāma's arrival released her.
At Mithilā Rāma lifts, strings and breaks the bow of Śiva that no king could lift, and Janaka, who found Sītā in a ploughed furrow, gives her to him.
After the four princes' weddings at Mithilā, Paraśurāma challenges Rāma with the bow of Vishnu; Rāma strings it, and Paraśurāma, recognising Vishnu, gives up his worlds won by penance.

object_literal: grieves for Sītā in spring at Lake Pampā
statement: In spring at Lake Pampā the beauty of the season deepens Rāma's grief for Sītā until Lakṣmaṇa urges him to take heart.

object_literal: greets Rāma disguised as an ascetic
statement: Sent by Sugrīva and disguised as an ascetic, Hanumān questions Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with such eloquence that Rāma praises his speech, and carries the brothers to Sugrīva.
Rāma and Sugrīva swear friendship around a sacred fire kindled by Hanumān; Sugrīva shows the ornaments Sītā dropped, which Rāma recognises, and Lakṣmaṇa knows only her anklets.
Sugrīva tells how, after he sealed the cave where Vālin pursued the asura Māyāvī and took the throne believing him dead, Vālin returned, drove him out and took his wife Rumā.

object_literal: shoots one arrow through seven sāl trees
statement: To convince Sugrīva of his strength, Rāma kicks Dundubhi's skeleton ten leagues with his toe and shoots an arrow through seven sāl trees, a mountain and the earth.
At the second duel, with Sugrīva marked by a garland, Rāma shoots Vālin in the chest from behind a tree after Vālin ignores Tārā's warning about Sugrīva's new ally.

The dying Vālin reproaches Rāma for shooting him from hiding; Rāma answers that Vālin deserved death for taking his brother's wife and that he was bound by his promise; Vālin accepts, entrusts Aṅgada to Sugrīva, and Tārā laments.

object_literal: forgets his promise during the rains
statement: Crowned king of Kiṣkindhā, Sugrīva spends the rains and the start of autumn in pleasure and forgets his promise, while Rāma waits on Mount Prasravaṇa longing for Sītā.

Sent by Rāma when Sugrīva forgets his promise, Lakṣmaṇa storms into Kiṣkindhā and shakes the palace with his bowstring; calmed by Tārā, he brings the repentant Sugrīva to Rāma as the monkey armies gather.

object_literal: receives Rāma's ring for Sītā
statement: Sugrīva sends search parties to the four quarters with a month's deadline; Rāma gives Hanumān, who goes south with Aṅgada and Jāmbavān, his ring engraved with his name as a token for Sītā.

object_literal: despairs with the southern search party
statement: The southern search party loses its month in the enchanted cave of the ascetic Svayamprabhā, who sends them to the southern ocean, where Aṅgada and the monkeys resolve to fast to death.

object_literal: is roused by Jāmbavān to leap the sea
statement: Jaṭāyu's brother Sampāti, whose wings regrow as he speaks, sees Sītā in Laṅkā a hundred leagues across the sea, and the bear-king Jāmbavān recounts Hanumān's birth and powers until he swells to the size of a mountain.

object_literal: leaps from Mount Mahendra and declines to rest
statement: Hanumān leaps from Mount Mahendra, shaking the mountain, and declines to rest on the golden mountain Maināka, which the Ocean raises for him in gratitude to the Ikṣvākus.

object_literal: passes Surasā's test and kills Siṃhikā
statement: Hanumān passes the test of Surasā by shrinking to a thumb's size and darting in and out of her widening mouth, and kills the shadow-seizing demoness Siṃhikā from within.
Shrunk to a cat's size, Hanumān enters Laṅkā by night and knocks down the city's guardian goddess, who recognises the sign Brahmā foretold of the rākṣasas' doom.

object_literal: searches Rāvaṇa's palace and mistakes Mandodarī for Sītā
statement: Searching Rāvaṇa's palace by night, Hanumān mistakes the sleeping queen Mandodarī for Sītā, then reasons that Sītā would never sleep adorned and at ease beside another man.
From a śiṃśapā tree in the aśoka grove Hanumān recognises Sītā, thin and unadorned among hideous rākṣasī guards, by Rāma's description and by ornaments matching those she had dropped.

When Rāvaṇa woos and threatens her in the aśoka grove, Sītā answers him across a blade of grass that she belongs to Rāma as light to the sun, and he leaves her two months before he will have her killed.

object_literal: is protected by Trijaṭā's dream of Rāma's victory
statement: When the rākṣasīs threaten to devour Sītā, the old rākṣasī Trijaṭā tells them of her dream of Rāma's triumph and Rāvaṇa's ruin, and they stop threatening her.

object_literal: sings Rāma's story to Sītā from the tree
statement: Seeing Sītā about to hang herself with her braid, Hanumān softly sings Rāma's story from the tree in ordinary speech so as not to frighten her.
Hanumān gives Sītā Rāma's ring; she refuses to be carried away on his back because she will not willingly touch another man and Rāma himself must rescue her, and gives him her crest-jewel as a token.

object_literal: tells the secret story of the crow as a token
statement: As a token known only to her and Rāma, Sītā tells Hanumān how Rāma once loosed Brahmā's weapon in a blade of grass against a crow, a son of Indra, that pecked her breast on Citrakūṭa.
Hanumān wrecks the aśoka grove, kills Rāvaṇa's guards, generals and son Akṣa, and lets himself be taken before Rāvaṇa after Indrajit binds him with the weapon of Brahmā.

Before Rāvaṇa, Hanumān declares himself Sugrīva's envoy and urges him to return Sītā since his boon does not protect him from men and monkeys; Vibhīṣaṇa saves him from execution because envoys may not be killed.
With his tail set alight by Rāvaṇa's order but made cool by Sītā's prayer to the fire god, Hanumān breaks free and burns Laṅkā, sparing Vibhīṣaṇa's house, and returns to find Sītā unharmed.
Hanumān leaps back across the sea, the monkeys celebrate in Sugrīva's honey grove, and he gives Rāma Sītā's crest-jewel, whereupon Rāma embraces him as the only reward equal to his deed.
After Hanumān's report on Laṅkā's defences, Rāma and Sugrīva march the army of monkeys and bears to the southern sea, Rāma riding on Hanumān's shoulders.
At Rāvaṇa's council Vibhīṣaṇa, citing ill omens, urges the return of Sītā and peace with Rāma, and is denounced by Rāvaṇa as a traitor to his house.

Over Sugrīva's objection that he is a spy, Rāma receives Vibhīṣaṇa on the principle that he protects anyone who seeks his refuge, even Rāvaṇa himself, and consecrates him king of Laṅkā with sea water.

object_literal: crosses to Laṅkā by the bridge built by Nala
statement: When the Ocean ignores his three-day fast, Rāma threatens it with his arrows until the Ocean rises and tells him that Nala, son of Viśvakarman, can build a bridge; the monkeys build it in five days and cross to Laṅkā.
Rāvaṇa tries to break Sītā with an illusory severed head of Rāma, and rejects the ultimatum brought by Aṅgada, who escapes after killing the rākṣasas sent to seize him.
Fighting invisibly from the clouds, Indrajit binds Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with serpent arrows until Garuḍa descends, the serpents flee and the brothers are healed.

object_literal: is woken to fight for his brother
statement: After Rāvaṇa is beaten and spared by Rāma, the giant Kumbhakarṇa, cursed to sleep for months, is woken with drums and a thousand elephants, rebukes his brother for taking Sītā, and goes out to fight for him.
After Kumbhakarṇa devours monkeys and carries off Sugrīva, Rāma shoots off his arms and legs, fills his mouth with arrows and cuts off his head with the arrow of Indra.

object_literal: brings the whole mountain of healing herbs
statement: When Indrajit's weapon of Brahmā fells the whole army, Hanumān, sent by Jāmbavān, tears up the Himalayan mountain of healing herbs and carries it to Laṅkā, reviving Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and the fallen army.

After Indrajit kills an illusory Sītā to break the besiegers' spirit, Lakṣmaṇa, guided by Vibhīṣaṇa, attacks him at the Nikumbhilā shrine before his sacrifice is complete and slays him with the arrow of Indra.
When Rāvaṇa strikes Lakṣmaṇa down with a dart given him by Maya, Hanumān carries Lakṣmaṇa back and, sent by the physician Suṣeṇa, again brings a mountain peak of herbs that heals him.
In Indra's chariot driven by Mātali, Rāma strikes off Rāvaṇa's regrowing heads a hundred times and finally kills him with Agastya's arrow charged with the weapon of Brahmā.

object_literal: is consecrated king of Laṅkā
statement: After Mandodarī's lament, Rāma tells Vibhīṣaṇa that enmity ends with death and bids him give Rāvaṇa a royal funeral; Vibhīṣaṇa is consecrated king of Laṅkā, and Sītā refuses to let Hanumān punish her rākṣasī guards.

object_literal: enters the fire to prove her faithfulness
statement: When Rāma rejects her in public for having lived in Rāvaṇa's house, Sītā answers that her heart was always his and her capture was not her fault, has Lakṣmaṇa build a pyre and enters the fire, praying to Agni.

Agni rises from the fire holding Sītā unharmed and declares her pure; Brahmā reveals Rāma as Nārāyaṇa and Sītā as Lakṣmī, Daśaratha appears from heaven, and Indra restores the fallen monkeys and bears.

object_literal: gives Rāma the flying chariot Puṣpaka
statement: Vibhīṣaṇa gives Rāma the flying chariot Puṣpaka; Rāma flies home with Sītā and his allies, showing her the places of their story, and sends Hanumān ahead to tell Bharata.

object_literal: is crowned king of Ayodhyā
statement: Bharata returns Rāma's sandals and kingdom, Rāma is consecrated king of Ayodhyā with Sītā beside him, Sītā gives her pearl necklace to Hanumān, and the epic describes the peace of Rāma's reign.
In autumn the pilgrims reach a red farmhouse where an old man tells them the only road west crosses eight hundred li of fire at the Flaming Mountains.

object_literal: one wave quenches the fire, two raise wind, three bring rain
statement: The villagers by the Flaming Mountains tell Sun Wukong that the plantain fan of the Iron Fan Immortal puts out the fire with one wave, raises wind with a second and brings rain with a third.
Princess Iron Fan, blaming Sun Wukong for losing her son Red Boy, strikes his head a dozen times with her swords when he asks to borrow the plantain fan, without hurting him.

object_literal: is fanned fifty thousand li and receives the wind-fixing pill
statement: Fanned fifty thousand li to the Little Sumeru Mountain by the plantain fan, Sun Wukong receives Lingji Bodhisattva's wind-fixing pill and returns to the Plantain Cave.
Unmoved by the fan thanks to the wind-fixing pill, Sun Wukong turns into an insect, is swallowed in Princess Iron Fan's tea and torments her from inside until she hands over a fan.

object_literal: discovers the fan is false
statement: Fanning the Flaming Mountains with the fan he took, Sun Wukong only makes the fire rise a thousand fathoms and burns his own hair, for the Rākṣasī had given him a false fan.

object_literal: formed from bricks of Laozi's furnace kicked over by Sun Wukong
statement: The earth god tells Sun Wukong that the Flaming Mountains came from bricks with live embers that fell when Wukong kicked over Laozi's furnace five hundred years before.
After Sun Wukong frightens the Jade-Faced Princess on Thunder Mountain, the Bull Demon King, his former sworn brother, comes out with an iron club, and they fight to a draw.

object_literal: steals the Bull Demon King's mount and takes his shape
statement: While the Bull Demon King feasts with the dragon king of the Green Wave Pool, Sun Wukong steals his golden-eyed water-parting beast and takes his form.
Disguised as the Bull Demon King, Sun Wukong is welcomed home by Princess Iron Fan, who tells him the first fan was false and spits out the real plantain fan, small as an apricot leaf.

object_literal: carries off the real fan but cannot shrink it
statement: Sun Wukong learns from Princess Iron Fan the spell that makes the plantain fan grow to twelve feet, reveals himself and leaves with it on his shoulder, not knowing how to shrink it.
The Bull Demon King takes Zhu Bajie's form, offers to carry the plantain fan for Sun Wukong and so tricks it back from him.
When the Bull Demon King, fighting Sun Wukong through many transformations, becomes a giant white ox, the guardian vajra kings surround him and Nezha burns him with his fire wheel until he submits.
With the plantain fan surrendered by Princess Iron Fan, Sun Wukong fans the Flaming Mountains forty-nine times, putting out the fire for good, and the pilgrims cross; he returns the fan to her.

object_literal: loses his attendants and is freed by the planet Venus
statement: On Double Fork Ridge Tang Sanzang falls into a demons' pit where the tiger spirit General Yin and his guests eat his two attendants; the planet Venus releases him at dawn.

object_literal: is sheltered by the hunter Liu Boqin
statement: The hunter Liu Boqin rescues Tang Sanzang from a tiger and takes him home; Sanzang's sutra chanting frees Boqin's dead father for rebirth, and Boqin escorts him to the Mountain of Two Frontiers.

object_literal: is freed from the Mountain of Two Frontiers
statement: Tang Sanzang lifts the Buddha's six-syllable seal from the Mountain of Two Frontiers, and Sun Wukong breaks out after five hundred years and kneels before him.

object_literal: slays the six robbers and leaves in anger
statement: Named Pilgrim Sun, Sun Wukong kills a tiger for its skin and slays six robbers named for the six senses; scolded by Tang Sanzang for killing, he leaves in anger.
Disguised as an old woman, Guanyin gives Tang Sanzang a cap with a golden band and the Tight-Fillet Spell; when Sun Wukong puts it on, the band takes root and the spell brings him to submission.

object_literal: is turned into the White Dragon Horse
statement: At Eagle Grief Gorge the jade dragon prince swallows Tang Sanzang's horse; Guanyin, called by the guardian spirits, turns him into the White Dragon Horse and gives Sun Wukong three life-saving hairs.

When the greedy abbot of a Guanyin Chan monastery tries to burn the pilgrims for their cassock, Sun Wukong shields his master with a borrowed fire-proof cover and fans the fire, during which a demon from Black Wind Mountain steals the cassock.

object_literal: keeps the stolen cassock for a robe feast
statement: The Black Bear Spirit of Black Wind Mountain keeps the stolen cassock for a birthday 'Buddha-robe feast' and holds off Sun Wukong, who goes to ask Guanyin for help.
Guanyin takes the form of the wolf Taoist Lingxuzi and offers Sun Wukong disguised as an elixir pill to the Black Bear Spirit, then subdues the bear with a fillet and makes him her mountain guardian.

object_literal: confronts the pig-faced son-in-law at Gao Village
statement: At Gao Village Sun Wukong takes the form of the daughter Cuilan to confront her pig-faced husband, who flees to Fuling Mountain when he recognises the Great Sage.

object_literal: joins Tang Sanzang and is named Bajie
statement: At the Cloud-Ladder Cave the pig-faced monster submits on hearing of the scripture pilgrimage, burns his cave and becomes Tang Sanzang's disciple, who names him Bajie.

object_literal: receives the Heart Sutra from the Crow's Nest Chan master
statement: On Pagoda Mountain the Crow's Nest Chan master teaches Tang Sanzang the Heart Sutra of fifty-four lines and 270 characters, which he memorises at a single hearing.

object_literal: has his eyes injured by the Samādhi wind
statement: At Yellow Wind Ridge the Tiger Vanguard seizes Tang Sanzang, and the Great King of the Yellow Wind blows a Samādhi wind that scatters Sun Wukong's clones and injures his fiery golden eyes.

object_literal: brings Lingji Bodhisattva to subdue the wind demon
statement: Healed by the guardian spirits' ointment and directed by the planet Venus, Sun Wukong brings Lingji Bodhisattva, whose flying-dragon staff pins the Yellow Wind demon — a yellow marten that had stolen lamp oil on Spirit Mountain.

object_literal: fights the demon of the Flowing Sands River
statement: At the Flowing Sands River Zhu Bajie fights the red-haired demon in the water while Sun Wukong waits on the bank; when the demon will not come ashore, Wukong goes to ask Guanyin for help.

object_literal: ferries the master across on a raft of nine skulls
statement: Called by name by Muzha, Sha Wujing submits to Tang Sanzang and ferries him across the Flowing Sands River on a raft of his nine skulls with Guanyin's gourd at the centre; the four pilgrims are now together.

object_literal: offers the three baskets of scripture to the east
statement: At the Ullambana feast the Buddha of the novel offers three baskets of scripture (35 works, 15,144 scrolls) for the eastern land and asks for a pilgrim to fetch them; Guanyin volunteers to find one.

object_literal: receives the cassock, staff and three fillets
statement: The Buddha gives Guanyin a brocade cassock, a nine-ringed staff and three fillets with spells for disciples who disobey; she sets out east with Huian (Muzha).

object_literal: is named Sha Wujing and told to wait for the pilgrim
statement: Guanyin enlists the banished Curtain-Raising General at the Flowing Sands River as Sha Wujing and the banished Marshal of the Heavenly Canopy at Fuling Mountain as Zhu Wuneng, to wait for the pilgrim.
