object_literal: spares the jade dragon and promises Wukong release
statement: Guanyin obtains a pardon for the condemned jade dragon prince to serve as the pilgrim's mount and promises Sun Wukong release if he becomes the pilgrim's disciple.

object_literal: father Chen Guangrui releases a golden carp
statement: In the novel's ninth chapter Tang Sanzang's father Chen Guangrui wins the examination, marries Yin Wenjiao through an embroidered ball and releases a blinking golden carp into the Hong River on his way to his post.

object_literal: father murdered at the Hong River crossing
statement: The boatman Liu Hong murders Chen Guangrui at the Hong River crossing and takes his post and his wife; the river's dragon king, the carp he had freed, preserves his body with a pearl.

object_literal: set adrift on a plank and raised at Jinshan Monastery
statement: As a newborn, Tang Sanzang is set adrift on a plank with his mother's letter in blood and the tip of his left little toe bitten off as a mark; Abbot Faming of Jinshan Monastery raises him as Jiangliu.

object_literal: finds his mother and avenges his father
statement: Ordained as Xuanzang at eighteen, he learns his origin from the blood letter, finds his mother, heals his blind grandmother, and his grandfather's troops capture Liu Hong; Chen Guangrui is restored to life by the river's dragon king.

object_literal: goes in disguise to test the fortune-teller
statement: Told by a yaksha that the fortune-teller Yuan Shoucheng guides the fisherman Zhang Shao's nets every day, the Dragon King of the Jing River goes into Chang'an disguised as a white-robed scholar to test him.

object_literal: alters heaven's rain decree to win a bet
statement: After betting against Yuan Shoucheng's forecast and then receiving a decree that matches it exactly, the Jing River dragon king delays the rain and withholds three inches and eight drops to win.

object_literal: is beheaded by Wei Zheng in a dream
statement: Though Emperor Taizong keeps Wei Zheng at chess to save him, the Jing River dragon king is beheaded at noon by Wei Zheng in a dream, and his head falls from the sky.

object_literal: dies after the dragon's ghost haunts him
statement: In the novel the beheaded dragon's ghost haunts Emperor Taizong; Qin Shubao and Yuchi Jingde guard his gate and become the door gods, and Taizong dies carrying Wei Zheng's letter to the underworld judge Cui Jue.

object_literal: visits the underworld and returns to life
statement: In the novel's underworld the judge Cui Jue changes Taizong's term in the register from the thirteenth to the thirty-third year; the emperor pays the wronged ghosts with a borrowed treasury, promises a mass for the dead and returns to life.

object_literal: sends Liu Quan's melons and repays Xiang Liang
statement: In the novel Liu Quan dies to deliver Taizong's melons to the underworld; his dead wife Li Cuilian returns in the body of the emperor's sister, and the emperor builds the Xiangguo Monastery for Xiang Liang.

object_literal: gives the cassock and staff for Xuanzang
statement: Disguised as a scabby monk, Guanyin offers the Buddha's cassock and staff for sale in Chang'an and then gives them free to Emperor Taizong for Xuanzang, chosen to lead the great mass for the dead.

object_literal: reveals her true form at the great mass
statement: At the great mass Guanyin interrupts Xuanzang's preaching of the Lesser Vehicle, announces the Great Vehicle scriptures at Thunderclap Monastery in the west and reveals her true form on a cloud.

object_literal: sets out west as Sanzang
statement: Xuanzang volunteers to fetch the scriptures; Emperor Taizong makes him his sworn brother, names him Sanzang and sends him west with a pinch of home soil in his wine.

object_literal: kills the two highwaymen chiefs
statement: When highwaymen tie Tang Sanzang to a tree, Sun Wukong tricks them into freeing him and kills their two chiefs; Sanzang buries them and prays that their ghosts blame Wukong alone.

object_literal: kills the robbers and beheads Old Yang's son
statement: When the son of their host Old Yang leads the robbers in pursuit, Sun Wukong kills the gang and brings the son's severed head to Tang Sanzang.
Horrified by the killings and the severed head of their host's son, Tang Sanzang recites the Tight-Fillet Spell repeatedly and drives Sun Wukong away.

object_literal: weeps before Guanyin at Potalaka
statement: Driven away a second time when he tries to return, Sun Wukong flies to Guanyin at Potalaka and weeps before her; she has no spell to loosen the fillet and keeps him with her.
In Sun Wukong's form, the false Monkey King offers Tang Sanzang water, is refused, knocks him senseless with an iron rod and flies off with the baggage and travel rescript.

object_literal: kills the false Sha Wujing on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit
statement: At the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit Sha Wujing finds the false Wukong reading the stolen travel rescript with a fake pilgrim party of monkeys; he kills the false Sha Wujing and flies to Guanyin.

object_literal: testifies that the real Wukong has been with her four days
statement: When Sha Wujing reaches Potalaka and finds Sun Wukong there, Guanyin testifies that Wukong has been with her for four days and sends the two of them to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit.
On the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit the false Monkey King, identical in every detail, fights the real Sun Wukong for hundreds of rounds while Sha Wujing cannot tell them apart.

object_literal: cannot tell the two Wukongs apart with the demon-revealing mirror
statement: Neither Guanyin's Tight-Fillet Spell, which pains both Wukongs alike, nor the demon-revealing mirror that Li Jing holds up before the Jade Emperor can tell the real Sun Wukong from the false.

object_literal: recites the spell but cannot tell the two Wukongs apart
statement: Tang Sanzang's Tight-Fillet Spell pains both Wukongs alike, and in the underworld the registers of the dead show no entry for either, since Wukong had long ago struck out the monkeys' names.

object_literal: is sent to the Buddha after Diting will not speak
statement: Kṣitigarbha's beast Diting hears the truth about the two Wukongs but will not name the false one to his face, and directs them to the Buddha because 'the Buddha's law is boundless'.
At Thunderclap Monastery the Buddha explains the four monkeys outside the ten categories of beings and names the false Wukong as the six-eared macaque, who hears and knows all things.
When the Buddha traps the six-eared macaque under his golden alms bowl, Sun Wukong kills him with one blow; Guanyin brings Wukong back to Tang Sanzang, who takes him back.

object_literal: covets Tang Sanzang's flesh on White Tiger Ridge
statement: On White Tiger Ridge, while Sun Wukong is away picking peaches, the White Bone Demon sees Tang Sanzang and resolves to trick him, believing that a bite of his flesh gives eternal life.

object_literal: strikes the demon disguised as a village girl
statement: Sun Wukong strikes the White Bone Demon disguised as a village girl offering food; she escapes leaving a false corpse, and when Zhu Bajie accuses Wukong of murder, Tang Sanzang recites the Tight-Fillet Spell.

object_literal: strikes the demon disguised as an old woman
statement: When the White Bone Demon returns as an eighty-year-old woman seeking her daughter, Sun Wukong strikes again; Tang Sanzang recites the spell twenty times but keeps him because there is no spell to loosen the fillet.
With the local gods standing witness so that she cannot escape, Sun Wukong kills the White Bone Demon disguised as an old man; she is revealed as a pile of bones inscribed 'Lady White Bone'.

object_literal: banishes Sun Wukong with a written dismissal
statement: Persuaded by Zhu Bajie that the bones are a trick, Tang Sanzang writes a letter of dismissal and banishes Sun Wukong, who bows to him from four sides with three magic copies and returns in tears to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit.
Back on the burned Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, Sun Wukong destroys the hunters who prey on his monkeys with a gale of stones, restores the mountain and raises the banner of the Great Sage again.
With Sun Wukong gone, Tang Sanzang wanders into a pagoda in the Black Pine Forest and is seized by the Yellow Robe Demon of the Moon-Wave Cave, who fights Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing to a standstill.

object_literal: carries the captive princess's letter to Baoxiang
statement: Princess Baihuaxiu of Baoxiang, held by the Yellow Robe Demon for thirteen years, persuades him to free Tang Sanzang and gives Sanzang a letter for her father.

object_literal: deserts the fight and leaves Sha Wujing to be captured
statement: Sent by the king of Baoxiang to rescue his daughter, Zhu Bajie boasts and grows huge at court, but in the fight with the Yellow Robe Demon he hides in a thicket, and Sha Wujing is captured.

object_literal: turns Tang Sanzang into a tiger
statement: Posing as the princess's rescuer and husband at the court of Baoxiang, the Yellow Robe Demon turns Tang Sanzang into a tiger with a spell and, drunk at the palace feast, eats a palace maid.

object_literal: attacks the demon disguised as a palace maid
statement: The White Dragon Horse takes the form of a palace maid, attacks the Yellow Robe Demon during a sword dance, is wounded by a candlestick and then urges Zhu Bajie to fetch Sun Wukong.

At the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit Zhu Bajie, rebuffed at first, goads Sun Wukong into returning by claiming the Yellow Robe Demon has insulted him; Wukong washes in the sea before going back to his master.
Disguised as Princess Baihuaxiu, Sun Wukong tricks the Yellow Robe Demon into giving up his inner elixir, swallows it and fights him until the demon vanishes.

object_literal: is revealed as the Kui Wolf star and recalled to heaven
statement: Checked against heaven's rolls, the Yellow Robe Demon is found to be the missing Kui Wolf star, who confesses that he came down to keep a promise to a jade maiden reborn as the princess and is sent to tend Laozi's furnace.
Sun Wukong breaks the spell on the caged tiger with a spray of water, restoring Tang Sanzang to human form; master and disciple are reconciled and the four pilgrims leave Baoxiang together.
Warned by an oracle against a man with one sandal, Pelias sees Jason arrive at his sacrifice having lost a sandal in the river Anaurus and sends him on the perilous voyage for the golden fleece.

object_literal: is built under Athena's direction and manned by the Argonauts
statement: The Argo is built by Argus under Athena's direction with a speaking beam of Dodonian oak, and some fifty heroes including Orpheus, Heracles, the Dioscuri and the sons of Boreas gather to sail with Jason.

object_literal: calms the heroes' quarrel with a song of the world's beginning
statement: After Heracles refuses the leadership and Jason is chosen, Orpheus calms a quarrel between Idas and Idmon at the parting feast with a song of how earth, heaven and sea were parted and Zeus came to rule.
On Lemnos, whose women had killed their menfolk, Queen Hypsipyle receives Jason and the Argonauts, who linger until Heracles rebukes them back to the ship.

object_literal: kills King Cyzicus in a night battle of mistaken identity
statement: Driven back by night to the land of the Doliones, the Argonauts fight their hosts unrecognised in the dark and Jason kills King Cyzicus, whose queen Cleite hangs herself; the storm abates only after sacrifice to Rhea.

object_literal: is drawn into a spring by a water-nymph
statement: In Mysia a water-nymph draws Hylas into a spring; Heracles and Polyphemus search for him and are left behind, and the sea god Glaucus declares that it is Zeus's will that Heracles return to his labours.

object_literal: kills the boxer-king Amycus
statement: Among the Bebrycians, whose king Amycus forces every stranger to box with him, Polydeuces kills Amycus with a blow above the ear and the Argonauts rout his people.

The sons of Boreas drive the Harpies from the blind seer Phineus until Iris swears by the Styx that they will not return, and Phineus in gratitude tells the Argonauts their route and how to pass the Clashing Rocks.
After a dove passes the Clashing Rocks losing only tail feathers, Athena holds back a rock with one hand and thrusts the Argo through with the other, and the rocks are fixed in place for ever.

object_literal: appears to the Argonauts at dawn on Thynias
statement: On the island of Thynias the Argonauts see Apollo pass at dawn on his way from Lycia to the Hyperboreans and build him an altar; in the land of the Mariandyni the seer Idmon is killed by a boar and the helmsman Tiphys dies of sickness.

object_literal: meets the shipwrecked sons of Phrixus on the island of Ares
statement: On the island of Ares the Argonauts roof the ship with their shields against birds that shoot their feathers, and rescue the shipwrecked sons of Phrixus, who agree to guide them to Colchis.

object_literal: arrives by night in the river Phasis in Colchis
statement: Passing the Caucasus, where they hear Prometheus's cries as the eagle flies to him, the Argonauts enter the Phasis by night, Jason pours libations to Earth and the gods of the land, and the ship is hidden in the reeds near the grove of the fleece.
At the request of Hera and Athena, Aphrodite promises Eros the golden ball Zeus played with as a child if he will shoot Medea with love for Jason.
In Aeetes's palace, as Chalciope welcomes her sons, Eros crouching at Jason's feet shoots Medea with an arrow that burns in her heart like fire.

Aeetes, suspecting a plot against his throne, sets Jason the trial of yoking fire-breathing bronze-footed bulls, ploughing the field of Ares, sowing a serpent's teeth and slaying the armed men who spring from them, all in one day.

object_literal: resolves after a sleepless night to give Jason a charm
statement: Through a sleepless night Medea wavers between helping Jason and loyalty to her father, agrees at Chalciope's plea to bring him a charm, contemplates poison in her shame, and turns back from death.

At Hecate's temple Medea gives Jason a charm made from the flower sprung from Prometheus's ichor and instructs him in the midnight sacrifice to Hecate, the anointing that makes him proof against fire and bronze, and the stone to throw among the earthborn men.

object_literal: yokes the fire-breathing bulls and destroys the earthborn men
statement: Protected by Medea's charm after his midnight sacrifice to Hecate, Jason yokes the fire-breathing bulls, ploughs the field of Ares, sows the serpent's teeth and, throwing a great stone among the earthborn men, destroys them as they fight one another.

Fearing her father, Medea flees to the Argonauts, receives Jason's oath of marriage, and lulls the sleepless serpent with song and a juniper sprig dipped in drugs so that Jason can take the golden fleece.
When Apsyrtus blocks the Argonauts' escape, Medea lures him with gifts to a night meeting at Artemis's temple island, where Jason kills him from ambush, incurring Zeus's wrath.

Warned by the Argo's speaking beam of Zeus's wrath, the Argonauts reach Aeaea by the Eridanus and Rhodanus, where Circe purifies Jason and Medea of Apsyrtus's blood with a suckling pig's blood and then drives Medea from her hall.
Orpheus drowns the Sirens' song with his lyre so that only Butes leaps overboard, rescued by Aphrodite, and Thetis and the Nereids toss the Argo from hand to hand past the Wandering Rocks.

When the Colchians demand Medea of the Phaeacians, Queen Arete warns Jason of Alcinous's judgment that only an unmarried maiden will be returned, and Jason and Medea are married that night in a sacred cave with the golden fleece spread on the bridal bed.

object_literal: is carried across the Libyan desert for twelve days
statement: Stranded in the Libyan Syrtis, the Argonauts follow the riddle of the heroines of Libya and carry the Argo on their shoulders for twelve days to Lake Tritonis, drinking at the spring Heracles struck near the garden of the Hesperides.
When the bronze giant Talos keeps the Argonauts from Crete with hurled rocks, Medea invokes the death-spirits and fixes him with her evil eye until he grazes the vein at his ankle and falls.

object_literal: lights the sea with his golden bow and reveals Anaphe
statement: In the Pall of Darkness after Crete, Apollo answers Jason's prayer and lights the sea with his golden bow, revealing the island the Argonauts name Anaphe; Euphemus's clod becomes Thera, and the heroes reach Pagasae.
When Zeus declares that the descendant of Perseus born that day will reign over Mycenae, Hera delays Alcmena's delivery and has Eurystheus born first as a seven-month child.
On the night before Amphitryon's return from the Taphian war, Zeus in his likeness lies with Alcmena and makes the night threefold; Alcmena bears Heracles to Zeus and Iphicles to Amphitryon.

object_literal: strangles in his cradle the serpents sent by Hera
statement: At eight months old Heracles strangles two huge serpents sent by Hera to his bed, while Iphicles cries out; Pherecydes says instead that Amphitryon put them there to learn which child was his.

object_literal: kills his lyre teacher Linus and is acquitted
statement: Taught chariot-driving, wrestling, archery, fighting in arms and the lyre by famous teachers, Heracles kills Linus with the lyre, is acquitted under the law of Rhadamanthys, and is sent to the cattle farm.

object_literal: kills the lion of Cithaeron
statement: At eighteen Heracles, entertained fifty days by Thespius, kills the lion of Cithaeron and thereafter wears its skin and gaping jaws.

object_literal: defeats the Minyans and marries Megara
statement: Heracles mutilates the heralds of Erginus who come for the Minyan tribute, defeats the Minyans for Thebes, in which war Amphitryon dies, and receives Megara from Creon and arms from the gods.

object_literal: is sent by the Delphic oracle to serve Eurystheus
statement: Driven mad by Hera, Heracles throws his own children and two of Iphicles's into the fire; the Pythia names him Heracles and orders him to serve Eurystheus at Tiryns for twelve years and perform the labours, promising immortality.

For his first labour Heracles chokes the invulnerable Nemean lion in a two-mouthed cave, sacrifices with Molorchus at Cleonae, and so frightens Eurystheus that the king hides in a bronze jar and sends orders by herald.

With Iolaus searing each severed neck, Heracles kills the nine-headed Lernaean hydra, buries its immortal head under a rock and poisons his arrows with its gall; Eurystheus refuses to count the labour because he had help.

object_literal: captures the golden-horned hind of Artemis after a year's hunt
statement: After hunting it for a year, Heracles captures the golden-horned Cerynitian hind sacred to Artemis at the river Ladon and appeases Artemis and Apollo by blaming Eurystheus.

object_literal: captures the Erymanthian boar after the fight with the centaurs
statement: On the way to the Erymanthian boar Heracles opens the centaurs' wine jar at Pholus's cave, fights the centaurs and accidentally wounds Chiron with a hydra-poisoned arrow; he then snares the boar in deep snow and brings it alive to Mycenae.

object_literal: cleanses Augeas's cattle-yard by diverting two rivers
statement: Heracles cleanses the cattle-yard of Augeas in one day by diverting the rivers Alpheus and Peneus through it; Augeas refuses the promised tenth of his cattle and Eurystheus refuses to count the labour as done for hire.

object_literal: drives off the Stymphalian birds with Athena's castanets
statement: With bronze castanets made by Hephaestus and given by Athena, Heracles frightens the Stymphalian birds out of their wood and shoots them down.

object_literal: captures the Cretan bull
statement: For his seventh labour Heracles captures the Cretan bull, said to be either Europa's bull or the bull Minos failed to sacrifice to Poseidon, and brings it to Eurystheus, who lets it go to roam to Marathon.

object_literal: brings the man-eating mares of Diomedes to Mycenae
statement: Heracles drives off the man-eating mares of the Thracian king Diomedes, kills Diomedes, founds Abdera at the grave of Abderus whom the mares devoured, and brings the mares to Eurystheus.
Hippolyte promises Heracles the belt of Ares, but Hera in the guise of an Amazon raises the cry that the queen is being abducted; Heracles, suspecting treachery, kills Hippolyte and takes the belt.

object_literal: saves Hesione at Troy and is cheated by Laomedon
statement: On the way back from the Amazons Heracles kills the sea monster sent by Poseidon against Troy and saves Hesione for the promised mares of Zeus, but Laomedon refuses payment and Heracles vows war.

object_literal: lends Heracles his golden goblet to cross Ocean
statement: On his way to Geryon Heracles sets up pillars at the bounds of Europe and Libya and, when he bends his bow at the scorching Sun, Helios in admiration lends him the golden goblet in which he crosses Ocean.
On Erytheia Heracles clubs the dog Orthus and the herdsman Eurytion, shoots Geryon by the river Anthemus, and ships the red cattle in the Sun's goblet to Tartessus.

object_literal: drives Geryon's cattle back to Greece
statement: Driving Geryon's cattle through Europe Heracles kills Ialebion, Dercynus and Eryx; Hera's gadfly scatters the herd in Thrace, and after eight years and a month Eurystheus imposes two more labours in place of the two he rejected.

object_literal: wrestles Nereus and kills Antaeus
statement: Seeking the Hesperides, Heracles holds the shape-shifting Nereus until he reveals the way, and in Libya lifts Antaeus, who draws strength from his mother Earth, off the ground and crushes him.
Heracles bursts his bonds at the altar of Busiris in Egypt, then in the Caucasus shoots the eagle that devours Prometheus's liver and frees him, receiving his advice to send Atlas for the apples.

object_literal: is tricked into taking back the sky
statement: Atlas fetches three golden apples of the Hesperides while Heracles holds the sky, wants to deliver them himself, and is tricked into taking back the sky when Heracles asks to put a pad on his head.

object_literal: descends to Hades and frees Theseus
statement: Initiated at Eleusis, Heracles descends at Taenarum, meets the shades of Meleager and Medusa, raises Theseus from the seat of forgetfulness but must leave Pirithous, and wrestles the herdsman Menoetes.

Permitted by Pluto to take Cerberus without weapons, Heracles masters the hound with his arms at the gates of Acheron, brings it up through Troezen to show Eurystheus, and returns it to Hades, completing the twelve labours.
Heracles outshoots Eurytus and his sons at Oechalia but is refused Iole, Eurytus fearing he would kill his children again; only Iphitus speaks for him.

object_literal: kills Iphitus by throwing him from the walls of Tiryns
statement: When Iphitus, who doubts that Heracles stole Eurytus's cattle, comes to him at Tiryns, Heracles in a renewed fit of madness throws him from the walls, and is afflicted with disease despite purification by Deiphobus.

Refused an oracle at Delphi, Heracles tries to carry off the tripod and fights Apollo until Zeus parts them with a thunderbolt; the oracle orders him sold into three years' servitude, and Hermes sells him to Omphale.
Serving Omphale, Heracles binds the Cercopes near Ephesus, kills Syleus who forced strangers to dig his vineyard, and buries Icarus; the Argonauts' voyage falls in these years.

object_literal: sacks Troy and kills Laomedon
statement: Heracles sacks Troy, spares Telamon who builds an altar to 'Heracles the Glorious Victor', shoots Laomedon and his sons, and lets Hesione ransom her brother Podarces with her veil, who is thereafter called Priam.

object_literal: fights beside the gods against the giants at Phlegra
statement: After Hera's storms drive him to Cos, Heracles is brought by Athena to Phlegra to fight beside the gods against the giants, then takes Elis, kills Augeas and celebrates the Olympian games, and sacks Pylos sparing only Nestor.
To win Deianira at Calydon, Heracles wrestles the river god Achelous in the form of a bull and breaks off his horn, which Achelous redeems with the horn of Amalthea.
Shot by Heracles at the river Evenus for assaulting Deianira, the dying centaur Nessus tells her to keep his blood from the wound as a love charm, which she does.
Heracles musters an army from Trachis, sacks Oechalia, kills Eurytus and his sons and takes Iole captive, then sends Lichas to fetch fine raiment for a sacrifice to Cenaean Zeus.
Believing Nessus's blood a love charm, Deianira smears a tunic with it; the hydra's poison eats Heracles's flesh as he sacrifices, he hurls Lichas into the sea, and Deianira hangs herself.

object_literal: is borne up to heaven from the pyre on Mount Oeta
statement: Heracles charges Hyllus to marry Iole, mounts a pyre on Mount Oeta which Poeas kindles and receives his bow for it, and is borne up to heaven by a cloud with a peal of thunder.
Made immortal, Heracles is reconciled with Hera and marries Hebe; on earth his sons find refuge at the Athenian altar of Mercy, and Hyllus kills the fleeing Eurystheus near the Scironian cliffs.

Hunting at Glyn Cuch, Pwyll drives off a pack of shining white red-eared hounds from their stag and is rebuked by their master, Arawn, king of Annwn, who asks him to rid him of his rival Hafgan in amends.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: In Arawn's shape Pwyll rules Annwn for a year in all its splendour, and every night turns his back to Arawn's queen and keeps faith with Arawn.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: kills Hafgan with a single blow and refuses a second
statement: At the ford Pwyll, in Arawn's shape, mortally wounds Hafgan with one blow and refuses to strike a second, so that Hafgan dies and his nobles submit, uniting Annwn under Arawn.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: Returning to Annwn, Arawn learns from his queen that Pwyll never touched her in the whole year, and he and Pwyll become firm friends, Pwyll being called Head of Annwn.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: Sitting on Gorsedd Arberth to see a wonder, Pwyll sees a lady on a white horse whom no rider can overtake though she rides slowly, until on the third day he calls on her to stop for the sake of the one she loves best.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: Rhiannon, daughter of Hefeydd the Old, chooses Pwyll over her betrothed, but at their wedding feast Pwyll rashly grants a boon to Gwawl son of Clud, who claims the bride, and Rhiannon devises a plan with a little bag.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: traps Gwawl in the magic bag and wins Rhiannon
statement: Disguised as a beggar, Pwyll asks Gwawl to fill Rhiannon's magic bag with food, traps Gwawl in it when he treads the food down, and releases him in the first game of Badger in the Bag on condition he renounce Rhiannon.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: When Rhiannon's newborn son vanishes in the night, her six sleeping attendants smear her with a staghound pup's blood and accuse her of devouring the child.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: sits at the gate of Arberth telling her tale and carrying guests
statement: Falsely accused, Rhiannon accepts the penance of sitting seven years by the horse-block at Arberth's gate, telling her tale to strangers and offering to carry them on her back into the court.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: is found by Teyrnon at his stable door and named Gwri Golden-hair
statement: Watching his mare on May Eve, Teyrnon cuts off a monstrous claw that seizes her foal through the window and finds an infant boy in satin at his door, whom he and his wife rear as Gwri Golden-hair.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: Seeing that the swiftly growing Gwri is the image of Pwyll and hearing of Rhiannon's penance, Teyrnon and his wife resolve to return the boy to Arberth.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: When Teyrnon brings the boy to Arberth and he is recognised as Pwyll's image, Rhiannon says she is delivered of her anxiety (pryder), and the boy is named Pryderi; he later rules Dyfed and marries Cigfa.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: From the rock of Harlech Bendigeidfran sees Matholwch's thirteen ships come in peace to ask for Branwen, and agrees to the match, held at Aberffraw in tents since no house can hold him.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: Insulted that Branwen was married without his consent, Efnysien maims Matholwch's horses, and Bendigeidfran makes amends with horses, a silver staff, a gold plate and the cauldron of rebirth.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: Pressed by his people to avenge the insult of the horses, Matholwch drives Branwen from his chamber to cook for the court, where the butcher strikes her daily, and bans all ships to Britain for three years.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: sends a starling to Britain with a letter of her sufferings
statement: Branwen rears a starling at her kneading-trough, teaches it to speak and sends it to Britain with a letter under its wing, and Bendigeidfran, reading it, musters the hosts of the island for war on Ireland.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: wades across the sea to Ireland
statement: Bendigeidfran wades across the sea to Ireland with his musicians on his back, and Branwen interprets the swineherds' vision: the forest is the ships' masts, the mountain her brother, the ridge his nose and the lakes his eyes.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: lies across the river as a bridge for his army
statement: When the Irish break the bridge over the river, Bendigeidfran says 'He who is a chief, let him be a bridge' and lies across it so that his host crosses over him; the Irish then offer the kingship to Gwern and build a house large enough to hold him.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: crushes the warriors hidden in the hundred bags
statement: Entering the great house before the host, Efnysien asks what is in each of the hundred bags hung on its pillars, is told 'meal', and crushes the head of the armed man hidden in each.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: throws Gwern into the fire
statement: After the peace is made and the kingship given to Branwen's son Gwern, Efnysien calls the child to him and throws him headlong into the fire, and war breaks out in the house as Bendigeidfran shields Branwen.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: Repenting as the Irish revive their dead in the cauldron of rebirth, Efnysien lies among the Irish dead, is thrown into the cauldron, and stretches himself until it bursts into four pieces and his own heart bursts.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: bids the seven survivors carry his severed head to London
statement: Wounded in the foot by a poisoned spear, Bendigeidfran bids the seven survivors cut off his head and carry it to the White Mount in London, foretelling seven years' feasting at Harlech and eighty at Gwales in its company.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: dies of a broken heart at Aber Alaw
statement: Landing at Aber Alaw and seeing both Ireland and Britain, Branwen laments that two good islands were laid waste because of her, and her heart breaks; she is buried in a four-sided grave by the Alaw.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: feasts with the wondrous head at Harlech and Gwales
statement: The seven survivors feast seven years at Harlech to the song of Rhiannon's birds and eighty years at Gwales with the uncorrupted head, until Heilyn opens the door facing Cornwall, their grief returns, and they bury the head in London.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: Seeing Manawydan homeless after Caswallon's usurpation, Pryderi gives him his mother Rhiannon in marriage and the rule of the seven cantrefs of Dyfed.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: finds Dyfed emptied by thunder and mist
statement: As Manawydan, Rhiannon, Pryderi and Cigfa sit on Gorsedd Arberth, a peal of thunder and a mist leave Dyfed emptied of all people, houses and beasts but themselves.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: excels as saddler and shield-maker and avoids a fight
statement: In England Manawydan and his companions make saddles at Hereford and then shields so well that the local craftsmen plot to kill them, and each time Manawydan restrains Pryderi from fighting and they move on.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: becomes one of the Three Golden Shoemakers
statement: Making shoes with gilded buckles so fine that he is called one of the Three Golden Shoemakers of Britain, Manawydan again avoids a fight with jealous craftsmen and returns with his companions to empty Dyfed.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: enters the enchanted fortress after the white boar
statement: Following a shining white boar that leads their hounds into a strange new fortress, Pryderi goes in after them against Manawydan's warning that the fortress is the work of whoever enchanted the land.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: Inside the fortress Pryderi and then Rhiannon take hold of a golden bowl hung by chains from the sky beside a fountain, stick fast and lose their speech, and vanish with the fortress in thunder and mist.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: swears to be a true companion to Cigfa and sows three crofts
statement: Left alone with Pryderi's wife Cigfa, Manawydan swears to be a true companion to her as to a daughter, makes shoes again in England, and returns to Dyfed with wheat to sow three crofts.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: watches mice carry off his wheat
statement: Finding two of his three crofts of wheat stripped of every ear overnight, Manawydan watches the third and sees a countless host of mice climb the stalks and carry off the ears.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: catches a pregnant mouse and resolves to hang it
statement: Manawydan catches a heavy, slow mouse in his glove and resolves to hang it despite Cigfa's protest that it is unseemly for a man of his rank.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: refuses the scholar's and priest's ransoms for the mouse
statement: As Manawydan sets up a gallows on Gorsedd Arberth to hang the mouse, a poor scholar offers a pound and a priest three pounds for its release, and he refuses both before a bishop arrives with his retinue.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: wins the release of Rhiannon, Pryderi and Dyfed as ransom for the mouse
statement: Refusing ever greater ransoms, Manawydan makes the bishop — Llwyd son of Cil Coed — release Rhiannon and Pryderi and lift the enchantment on Dyfed, and learns that the mouse is Llwyd's wife and the enchantment was vengeance for Gwawl and the Badger in the Bag.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: is restored from captivity with the asses' collars
statement: Having sworn Llwyd to take no vengeance, Manawydan sees Rhiannon and Pryderi restored and the people and herds of Dyfed returned, learning that in captivity Pryderi wore the gate-knockers and Rhiannon the asses' collars.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: To draw Math away from his footholder Goewin, whom Gilfaethwy desires, Gwydion comes to Pryderi's court as a bard and exchanges illusory horses, hounds and shields made from fungus for Pryderi's swine from Annwn.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: While Math is at war, Gilfaethwy violates Goewin; when Pryderi proposes single combat to spare their people, Gwydion kills him at Maen Tyriawg by strength and magic.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: Learning of Goewin's violation, Math marries her to spare her shame and with his wand turns Gilfaethwy and Gwydion into a pair of deer, then swine, then wolves for three years before restoring them.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: drops two children as she steps over Math's wand
statement: Stepping over Math's magic wand as a test of maidenhood, Arianrhod drops a yellow-haired boy, baptised as Dylan son of the Wave, and something small that Gwydion hides in a chest.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: When Arianrhod swears her son shall have no name but from her, Gwydion brings him disguised as shoemakers' boy, and when the boy strikes a wren between sinew and bone she laughs at the fair one's skilful hand, giving him the name Lleu Llaw Gyffes.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: When Arianrhod swears Lleu shall bear no arms unless she arms him, Gwydion comes with him as bards, conjures an illusory fleet attacking Caer Arianrhod, and she arms Lleu herself.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: When Arianrhod swears Lleu shall have no wife of the race now on earth, Math and Gwydion make Blodeuedd from the blossoms of oak, broom and meadowsweet, and she marries Lleu, who rules Dinoding from Mur Castell.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: falls in love with Gronw Pebr and plots against Lleu
statement: While Lleu is away, Blodeuedd shelters Gronw Pebr, lord of Penllyn, after his hunt, falls in love with him, and plots with him to learn how Lleu may be killed.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: is struck by Gronw's spear and flies away as an eagle
statement: Lleu tells Blodeuedd he can be slain only by a spear a year in the making, on a riverbank under a thatched roof with one foot on a bath and the other on a he-goat; when he shows her the posture, Gronw's spear strikes him and he flies away as an eagle.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: Following a sow to an oak where she feeds on flesh falling from an eagle, Gwydion sings three englynion that bring the eagle down to his knee and restores Lleu to human form with his wand.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

statement: As Blodeuedd flees and her maidens drown in Llyn y Morwynion, Gwydion overtakes her and turns her into an owl that will never dare show itself by day and that all birds will mob.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: kills Gronw Pebr with a spear through the stone
statement: Refusing compensation, Lleu has Gronw Pebr stand where he himself stood when struck; Gronw shelters behind a stone, but Lleu's spear pierces the stone and kills him, and the stone is called Llech Gronw.
tradition_scope: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Guest translation)

object_literal: imprisons Danaë in a bronze chamber after the oracle
statement: Warned by an oracle that his daughter's son would kill him, Acrisius imprisons Danaë in an underground bronze chamber, where Zeus visits her as a shower of gold and she bears Perseus.

object_literal: is cast into the sea in a chest with Perseus and rescued by Dictys
statement: Acrisius casts Danaë and the infant Perseus into the sea in a chest, which washes ashore on Seriphos, where Dictys takes them in and rears the boy.
Wanting Danaë, King Polydectes tricks Perseus at a feast for bridal gifts into undertaking to bring him the Gorgon's head.
Guided by Hermes and Athena, Perseus seizes the single eye and tooth shared by the three Phorcides and returns them only when they show him the way to the nymphs.

object_literal: receives winged sandals, the kibisis and the cap of Hades
statement: The nymphs give Perseus winged sandals, the kibisis wallet and the cap of Hades, and Hermes gives him an adamantine sickle, with which he flies to the Gorgons at Ocean.

object_literal: is found asleep with her immortal sisters by Ocean
statement: Perseus finds the three Gorgons, Stheno, Euryale and the mortal Medusa, asleep by Ocean; the Library describes their dragon-scaled heads, tusks, bronze hands and golden wings and their petrifying gaze.

Looking at Medusa's reflection in a bronze shield with Athena guiding his hand, Perseus beheads her; Pegasus and Chrysaor spring from her neck, and the cap of Hades hides him from her pursuing sisters.
In Ethiopia Perseus finds Andromeda exposed to a sea monster sent by Poseidon after Cassiepea's boast, wins the oath of her parents that she will be his wife, kills the monster and frees her.

object_literal: petrifies Phineus and his fellow conspirators
statement: When Phineus, Andromeda's former betrothed, plots against him, Perseus shows the Gorgon's head and turns Phineus and his fellow conspirators to stone.
Finding Danaë and Dictys driven to the altars by Polydectes's violence, Perseus turns Polydectes and his friends to stone with the Gorgon's head and makes Dictys king of Seriphos.

object_literal: sets the Gorgon's head in the middle of her aegis
statement: Perseus returns the sandals, wallet and cap through Hermes to the nymphs and gives the Gorgon's head to Athena, who sets it in the middle of her aegis.
At funeral games in Larissa Perseus's discus strikes and kills Acrisius, fulfilling the oracle; ashamed to claim Argos, Perseus exchanges it for Tiryns and fortifies Midea and Mycenae.

object_literal: is preceded by the Fimbulwinter and three winters of kin-slaying war
statement: Gylfaginning 51 says Ragnarök will be preceded by three winters of world-wide war in which kin kill kin, and by the Fimbulwinter, three winters together with no summer between.

object_literal: breaks loose when every fetter breaks
statement: In Gylfaginning 51 the wolf swallows the sun and the other seizes the moon, the stars vanish, the earth quakes so that every fetter breaks, and Fenrir runs free.

object_literal: is loosed in the flood and steered by Hrymr
statement: In Gylfaginning 51 the sea surges ashore as the Midgard serpent writhes, and Naglfar, made of dead men's nails, is loosed in the flood and steered by the giant Hrymr, while Fenrir advances with jaws from earth to sky.

object_literal: leads the sons of Muspell across the breaking Bifröst
statement: In Gylfaginning 51 the sky splits and Surtr leads the sons of Muspell with fire before and behind him and a sword brighter than the sun; Bifröst breaks beneath them, and they gather with the giants and Hel's host on the plain of Vígríðr.
In Gylfaginning 51 Heimdall blows a mighty blast on the Gjallarhorn and wakes the gods, Odin rides to Mímir's well for counsel, Yggdrasil trembles, and the Æsir and einherjar arm for battle.
In Gylfaginning 51 Odin with golden helmet and Gungnir goes against Fenrir, Thor beside him must fight the Midgard serpent, and Freyr falls to Surtr for lack of the sword he gave to Skírnir.
In Gylfaginning 51 Garmr and Týr kill each other, and Thor kills the Midgard serpent but steps away only nine paces before falling dead from its poison.

In Gylfaginning 51 Fenrir swallows Odin, and Víðarr, wearing the shoe made of all the leather scraps ever cut, sets his foot in the wolf's lower jaw and tears its mouth apart; Loki and Heimdall kill each other.

object_literal: flings fire over the earth and burns the whole world
statement: In Gylfaginning 51 Surtr flings fire over the earth and burns the whole world, and Snorri quotes the Seeress's Prophecy: the sun turns black, the earth sinks into the sea and the stars fall.

object_literal: is followed by abodes of reward and punishment
statement: Gylfaginning 52 describes the abodes after Ragnarök: Gimlé, Brimir and Sindri for the good, and Náströnd's hall woven of serpents' spines, where oath-breakers and murderers wade rivers of poison, and Hvergelmir, where Níðhöggr torments the dead.

object_literal: returns from Hel to the renewed world
statement: In Gylfaginning 53 the earth rises green from the sea; Víðarr, Váli, Móði and Magni survive, Baldr and Höðr return from Hel, the gods find the golden chess pieces, Líf and Lífþrasir repeople the world, and the sun's daughter drives her mother's course.

object_literal: ends Gangleri's questioning as the hall vanishes
statement: At the close of Gylfaginning (53–54) the speaker says no one can tell more of the world's future, the hall vanishes around Gangleri leaving him on an open plain, and he returns to tell the stories.

In the pillow-talk at Cruachan, Medb and Ailill count their possessions and find them equal except for the White-horned Bull Finnbennach, born in Medb's herd but gone over to Ailill's, which Medb cannot match.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

statement: Medb sends Mac Roth to borrow the Brown Bull of Cúailnge from Dáire mac Fiachna, who agrees until a drunken messenger boasts it would have been taken by force, whereupon Dáire refuses and Medb resolves to take it.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

object_literal: hears Fedelm's prophecy of red ruin
statement: Before the host sets out from Cruachan, the prophetess Fedelm tells Medb 'I see it crimson, I see it red' and sings of a young warrior who will destroy her army alone.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

object_literal: leads Medb's host astray to give Ulster time
statement: While the Ulstermen lie under Macha's curse of debility and Cú Chulainn alone guards the border, Fergus leads Medb's host astray to give Ulster time, and persuades Medb to scatter the outstanding Gailióin through the host instead of killing them.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

object_literal: halts the host with the ogam withe and the forked branch
statement: Cú Chulainn halts Medb's host with an ogam-inscribed withe twisted with one hand, one foot and one eye, and with a four-pronged fork driven one-handed into a ford bearing the heads of four scouts, which only Fergus can pull out.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

statement: Fergus tells Medb and Ailill how the boy Sétanta, not yet five, came alone to Emain Macha, warded off the hundred and fifty boys of the boy-troop and was taken in by King Conchobar.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

object_literal: kills Culann's hound and receives the name Cú Chulainn
statement: As a boy Sétanta kills the smith Culann's ferocious hound with his ball and a standing stone, offers to guard Culann's house himself until a whelp is grown, and is named Cú Chulainn, 'the hound of Culann', by the druid Cathbad.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

object_literal: takes arms on the day of Cathbad's prophecy
statement: Hearing Cathbad say that whoever takes arms that day will be famous but short-lived, the boy Cú Chulainn takes Conchobar's own arms and chariot, kills the three sons of Nechta Scéne, and is cooled from his battle-fury in three vats of water.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

object_literal: fights champion after champion at the ford
statement: Cú Chulainn agrees with Medb to fight one champion a day at the ford while the host advances only during the combat, drowns Fráech and kills many others, and gives way before Fergus on his promise to yield in return one day.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

statement: Refused by Cú Chulainn when she offers her love as a king's daughter, the Morrígan attacks him as eel, wolf and heifer during his fight with Lóch and is wounded thrice, then is healed by his blessings as she gives him milk as an old woman.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

statement: At Lerga, Lug mac Ethnenn comes from the síd unseen through the host, tells the wounded Cú Chulainn that he is his father, and heals him with herbs of the síd while he sleeps three days and nights.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

object_literal: loses his son Follomain with the boy-troop of Emain
statement: While Cú Chulainn sleeps under Lugh's care, the boy-troop of Emain led by Conchobar's son Follomain attacks Medb's host three times and is slain to the last boy.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

object_literal: makes the Great Slaughter in his battle-distortion
statement: To avenge the boy-troop, Cú Chulainn in his ríastrad, the monstrous battle-distortion, drives his scythed chariot round the host of the four provinces in the Great Slaughter on the plain of Muirthemne.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

statement: Medb forces Fer Diad, Cú Chulainn's foster-brother and fellow pupil of Scáthach, to fight him by threatening him with poets' satire and promising her daughter Finnabair, land and freedom from tribute.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

statement: On the first day at the ford Fer Diad and Cú Chulainn fight with casting-weapons from morning to evening, then embrace, and that night share healing herbs and food, their horses in one paddock and their charioteers at one fire.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

statement: On the second day Cú Chulainn and Fer Diad fight with heavy spears from their chariots and still exchange courtesies at night; on the third, with heavy swords, after which they part without embracing.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

statement: On the fourth day at the ford, as Fer Diad's sword pierces him, Cú Chulainn calls for the Gáe Bulga, casts it from between his toes through Fer Diad's iron and stone, and Fer Diad dies in his arms.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

object_literal: laments Fer Diad at the ford
statement: Cú Chulainn carries the dead Fer Diad across the ford to the northern bank, faints beside him, and laments that all fighting before had been play and pleasure until he met Fer Diad.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

object_literal: rouses Ulster after Sualtam's severed head cries out
statement: When Sualtam, beheaded by the rim of his own shield as his horse wheels, still cries from the shield that Ulster's men are slain, women carried off and cattle driven, Conchobar swears to restore them all and the Ulstermen rise from their debility.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

object_literal: names the Ulster companies as Mac Roth describes them
statement: As the risen Ulstermen march on the plain of Gárech, Mac Roth describes each approaching company to Medb and Ailill, and the exiled Fergus names their leaders.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

statement: In the battle of Gárech Fergus strikes Conchobar's shield with Caladbolg until a warrior (in some versions Cormac Cond Longas) persuades him to turn his wrath on the hills, and he strikes the tops from three hills, the three Maela of Meath.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

statement: Hearing Caladbolg strike Conchobar's shield, Cú Chulainn bursts his bonds and calls on Fergus to keep his promise; Fergus retreats three steps, and his exiles and the men of Leinster and Munster leave the field.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

statement: With the host routed and the Brown Bull sent ahead to Connacht, Cú Chulainn finds Medb on her retreat, spares her because he will not kill a woman, and guards her until the host crosses Áth Luain.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

statement: Brought to Connacht, the Brown Bull of Cúailnge fights the White-horned Bull Finnbennach through a whole night across Ireland, trampling the judge Bricriu, and is seen at dawn with Finnbennach's remains on its horns.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

object_literal: dies on Druim Tairb when its heart breaks
statement: Scattering Finnbennach's remains across Ireland, giving names to places such as Áth Luain, the Brown Bull returns to Cúailnge and dies on Druim Tairb when its heart breaks, and peace is made for seven years.
tradition_scope: Táin Bó Cúalnge, Book of Leinster recension (Dunn translation)

object_literal: leads his outlawed son Sigi to a new kingdom
statement: When his son Sigi kills the thrall Breði in jealousy and is outlawed, Odin leads him out of the land and gives him warships, and Sigi wins the kingdom of Hunland.

object_literal: is born after six years and builds his hall round the Branstock
statement: Born after six years in the womb of a mother who conceived by eating Odin's apple brought by the wish-maiden Hljóð, Völsungr becomes king, marries Hljóð and builds his hall round the oak Branstock.

object_literal: draws Odin's sword from the Branstock
statement: At Signý's wedding feast a one-eyed stranger drives a sword into the Branstock; only Sigmundr can draw it, and his refusal to sell it to Siggeir for three times its weight in gold makes Siggeir his enemy.

object_literal: falls in Gautland keeping his vow never to flee
statement: Warned by Signý of Siggeir's treachery, Völsungr refuses to flee, keeping the vow he swore before his birth never to flee fire or iron, and falls in battle in Gautland while his ten sons are captured.

object_literal: bites out the she-wolf's tongue and escapes
statement: After a she-wolf, said to be Siggeir's mother, devours his nine brothers in the stocks on nine nights, Sigmundr, his face smeared with honey by Signý's messenger, bites out the wolf's tongue and escapes into the forest.

object_literal: tests her sons by Siggeir and finds them unfit for vengeance
statement: Testing her two sons by Siggeir for courage, Signý finds them afraid and has Sigmundr kill them, resolving that only a pure Völsung could be an avenger.

object_literal: is born to Signý by Sigmundr and passes the test of courage
statement: Born to Signý by Sigmundr after she exchanged shapes with a sorceress, Sinfjötli endures his mother's test without flinching and kneads a venomous serpent into the bread Sigmundr sets him to make.
Wearing enchanted wolf-skins with Sinfjötli, Sigmundr in anger bites him in the throat when he fights eleven men alone, then heals him with a leaf a raven brings, and they burn the skins.

object_literal: returns into the burning hall to die with Siggeir
statement: When Sigmundr and Sinfjötli, buried alive by Siggeir, cut through the mound's dividing slab with the sword Signý throws in hidden in pork and burn Siggeir's hall, Signý reveals Sinfjötli's parentage and goes back into the fire to die with her husband.

object_literal: is poisoned and carried off by a mysterious ferryman
statement: Poisoned by Borghildr at her brother's funeral feast after Sigmundr, drunk, tells him to strain the drink through his beard, Sinfjötli dies, and a mysterious ferryman takes his body and vanishes.
In Sigmundr's last battle against Lyngvi, a one-eyed man in a blue cloak holds up his spear against Sigmundr's stroke and the sword breaks in two, and Sigmundr falls mortally wounded.

Dying, Sigmundr refuses healing because Odin has broken his sword and tells Hjördís to keep the shards for their unborn son, from which the sword Gram will be made; Hjördís is taken in by Álfr and bears Sigurðr.
Fostered by the smith Reginn at King Hjálprekr's court, Sigurðr chooses the grey horse Grani of Sleipnir's kin by driving the herd into a river on the advice of a long-bearded old man, who is Odin.

object_literal: kills Otr in otter shape and brings on the gods the otter-ransom
statement: In Reginn's tale Loki kills Otr, son of Hreiðmarr, in otter shape at Andvari's falls with a stone, and Hreiðmarr seizes Odin, Loki and Hœnir until they agree to fill and cover the otter-skin with gold.
Caught as a pike in Rán's net by Loki, the dwarf Andvari gives up his gold and the ring Andvaranautr, and curses both to be the death of everyone who owns them.

object_literal: kills his father for the gold and becomes a dragon at Gnitaheiðr
statement: After Odin covers the last whisker of the otter-skin with Andvaranautr and Loki repeats the curse, Fáfnir kills his father Hreiðmarr for the gold and becomes a dragon lying on it at Gnitaheiðr.

object_literal: is reforged from Sigmundr's shards and cleaves the anvil
statement: After two swords Reginn forges break on the anvil, he forges Gram from Sigmundr's shards, and Sigurðr cleaves the anvil to its base with it and cuts a tuft of wool drifting in the river.

object_literal: avenges Sigmundr on the sons of Hundingr
statement: After Grípir foretells his fate, Sigurðr sails against the sons of Hundingr, takes aboard the stranger Hnikarr who stills the storm, and kills Lyngvi and his brothers, avenging his father.

Advised by a long-bearded old man to dig trenches for the blood as well as the pit Reginn proposed, Sigurðr stabs Fáfnir from below under the left shoulder up to the hilt as the dragon crawls to the water.
Dying, Fáfnir draws out Sigurðr's name, warns him that the gold and the ring will be his bane and that Reginn will betray him, and answers his questions about the Norns and the last battle.

Tasting Fáfnir's heart-blood as he roasts the heart, Sigurðr understands the nuthatches warning him of Reginn's treachery, beheads Reginn with Gram, and loads the dragon's hoard and the helm of terror onto Grani.

On Hindarfjall Sigurðr cuts open the mail of a sleeping warrior in a shield-burg and wakes Brynhildr, whom Odin had pricked with a sleep-thorn for giving victory against his will, and who had vowed to wed only a man who knew no fear.

object_literal: teaches Sigurðr the runes and swears oaths with him
statement: Brynhildr gives Sigurðr a horn of mead and teaches him victory-runes, ale-runes, help-runes, sea-runes, limb-runes, speech-runes and mind-runes with counsels for life, and they swear oaths to each other.
At Hlymdalir Sigurðr sees Brynhildr through a tower window weaving his deeds in gold; though she foretells he will marry Guðrún, they renew their oaths and he gives her the ring Andvaranautr.

Brynhildr interprets Guðrún's dreams of a golden hawk and a golden hart, foretelling that she will marry Sigurðr through her mother's guile, lose him through Brynhildr, then marry Atli and lose her brothers.
At Gjúki's court Queen Grímhildr gives Sigurðr a magic drink that makes him forget Brynhildr; he marries Guðrún and swears blood-brotherhood with Gunnarr and Högni under a strip of turf.
When Gunnarr's horse shies from the fire round Brynhildr's hall and Grani will not move under him, he and Sigurðr exchange shapes by the craft Grímhildr taught them.

In Gunnarr's shape Sigurðr rides Grani through Brynhildr's fire, claims her by her vow, lies three nights with the naked Gram between them, and takes from her the ring Andvaranautr, giving her another.

object_literal: remembers his oaths to Brynhildr after her wedding to Gunnarr
statement: At the end of Gunnarr and Brynhildr's wedding feast Sigurðr remembers all his oaths to Brynhildr, but, married to Guðrún and bound to his sworn brother, he keeps silent.

When Brynhildr claims precedence while washing their hair in the Rhine, Guðrún reveals that Sigurðr, not Gunnarr, rode through the fire and shows her the ring Andvaranautr, and Brynhildr goes home pale and silent.
Brynhildr lies silent for days, then reproaches Gunnarr for winning her by deceit, condemns Grímhildr's drink of forgetfulness and curses the house of Gjúki as oath-breakers.

Sigurðr tells Brynhildr he forgot her through the drink and offers to leave Guðrún for her, but she refuses to have two husbands in one hall, and his grief bursts the rings of his mail-coat as he leaves.
Pressed by Brynhildr's false charge, Gunnarr, bound with Högni by oaths of brotherhood, has their brother Guttormr, fed on wolf and serpent flesh, kill Sigurðr in his bed on the third morning.
Mortally wounded, Sigurðr hurls Gram after Guttormr and cuts him in two, declares to Guðrún that he never wronged Gunnarr or betrayed their oath, and dies, while Brynhildr laughs at Guðrún's wailing.

object_literal: laments Sigurðr over his body
statement: Guðrún sits dry-eyed by Sigurðr's body until her sister lays his bloodied head in her lap, and then she weeps and laments that he stood among Gjúki's sons like a tall leek above the grass.
Having foretold the fall of Gjúki's house, Brynhildr stabs herself and asks to be burned on Sigurðr's pyre with a naked sword between them as in their three nights, and they are burned together.

object_literal: floats on the primeval sea; the world is made from the duck's broken eggs
statement: Kalevala Rune I says Ilmatar, daughter of the air, floated on the sea as Water-mother, that a duck laid six golden eggs and one of iron on her raised knee, and that the broken eggs became the earth, the sky, the sun, the moon, the stars and the clouds.

Kalevala Rune I says Ilmatar shaped the headlands, bays and shores, and that Väinämöinen, after thirty summers in her womb, forced his way out, drifted on the sea for years and came ashore already old.

object_literal: has the forests sown, the great oak felled and the barley grown
statement: Kalevala Rune II says Väinämöinen had Sampsa Pellervoinen sow the forests, that a little man from the sea grew into a giant and felled the oak that hid the sun and moon, and that Väinämöinen cleared the land for barley, sparing a birch for the birds.

Kalevala Rune III says that when the young Joukahainen challenged Väinämöinen to a contest of wisdom and then to a fight, Väinämöinen sang his sledge, horse and weapons into other shapes and sank him into a swamp up to his chin.

Kalevala Runes III–IV say that Joukahainen, sinking in the swamp, offered bows, boats, horses, gold and fields and at last his sister Aino, whereupon Väinämöinen sang him free; his mother rejoiced, but Aino wept.

object_literal: drowns rather than marry the old Väinämöinen
statement: Kalevala Rune IV says Aino, refusing to marry the old Väinämöinen, swam out to a rock in the sea that sank with her, and that her mother's tears became three rivers by which three birches and three cuckoos appeared.

Kalevala Rune V says Väinämöinen caught a strange fish that leapt back into the sea and told him it was Aino, whom he had failed to recognise, and that his dead mother then advised him to seek a bride in Pohjola.

Kalevala Rune VI says Joukahainen lay in wait with a steel bow against his mother's warning, and that his third arrow struck Väinämöinen's horse so that Väinämöinen fell into the sea and was swept away.

Kalevala Rune VII says an eagle, remembering the birch he spared, carried Väinämöinen to Pohjola, where Louhi promised to send him home and give her daughter for the forging of a Sampo, which he said only Ilmarinen could make.

Kalevala Rune VIII says the maiden of Pohjola, weaving on the rainbow, set Väinämöinen impossible tasks, and that while building a boat from her spindle his axe, misguided by evil spirits, cut deep into his knee.

Kalevala Rune IX says an old man healed Väinämöinen's knee after Väinämöinen told the origin of iron — born of three maidens' milk, forged by Ilmarinen and made fierce when Hiisi's hornet poisoned the tempering water.

Kalevala Rune X says Väinämöinen tricked Ilmarinen into going to Pohjola, where after rejecting a bow, a boat, a heifer and a plough he forged the Sampo with its many-coloured lid, which Louhi locked in her stone mountain while the maiden refused him.
Kalevala Rune XI says the reckless Lemminkäinen went to the island of Saari to woo Kyllikki, who had refused the sons of the sun, moon and stars, and befriended all the island maidens except her.
Kalevala Rune XI says Lemminkäinen carried Kyllikki off in his sledge, and that they swore before Ukko that he would never go to war and she would never go dancing in the village.

Kalevala Rune XII says Kyllikki broke her vow and went dancing in the village while Lemminkäinen was fishing, and that when his sister Ainikki told him he declared himself free of his own oath and set out for Pohjola.
Kalevala Rune XII says that, ignoring his mother's warnings, Lemminkäinen threw down his brush saying that when it dripped blood misfortune would have befallen him, and drove north to Pohjola.
Kalevala Rune XII says Lemminkäinen sang all the sorcerers of Pohjola away except the old blind herdsman Märkähattu, whom he mocked, and who went in hatred to wait by the river of Tuonela.
Kalevala Rune XIII says Louhi set Lemminkäinen the task of catching the elk of Hiisi on skis, and that he chased the elk Hiisi had made into Lapland until his ski and pole broke and the elk escaped.

object_literal: catches the elk of Hiisi after praying to the forest gods
statement: Kalevala Rune XIV says that after praying for three days to the forest gods Tapio and Mielikki, Lemminkäinen caught the elk of Hiisi and brought it to Louhi, who then set him a second task.
Kalevala Rune XIV says that when Louhi set him to bridle Hiisi's fire-breathing gelding, Lemminkäinen prayed Ukko to quench it with hail and then bridled it with a golden halter.

Kalevala Rune XIV says that when Lemminkäinen went to shoot the swan of Tuonela, the blind herdsman Märkähattu, lying in wait, pierced his heart with a water-serpent, and he lamented that he had never learned the charm against it.
Kalevala Rune XIV says the herdsman threw the dying Lemminkäinen into the black river of Tuonela, where the son of Tuoni hewed him into pieces and cast them into its depths.

Kalevala Rune XV says that when the brush dripped blood Lemminkäinen's mother hurried to Pohjola, forced Louhi to tell where she had sent him, and after the trees, the road and the moon could not help, learned from the sun that he lay hewn in pieces in the river of Tuonela.

Kalevala Rune XV says Lemminkäinen's mother raked her son's body piece by piece from the river of Tuonela with a copper rake forged by Ilmarinen, had his veins joined, and revived him with the Creator's honey brought by a bee from beyond the nine heavens.
Kalevala Rune XXXI says the brothers Untamo and Kalervo quarrelled over a run of petty matters until Untamo slew Kalervo's people, sparing only a pregnant woman whom he took as a slave.

Kalevala Rune XXXI says Kullervo, born to the captive woman in Untamo's house, broke his swaddling and cradle in his third month and was heard vowing to avenge his father, so that Untamo resolved to kill him.

Kalevala Rune XXXI says Untamo tried to kill the young Kullervo in a barrel thrown into the lake, on a burning pyre and hanged from an oak, and each time found him alive — fishing, stirring the embers, carving warriors on the tree.

Kalevala Rune XXXI says Kullervo ruined every task Untamo set him — minding a child, clearing the forest, building a fence, threshing the rye — and that Untamo sold him to the smith Ilmarinen in Karelia for worn-out kettles and old tools.
Kalevala Rune XXXII says Ilmarinen's wife sent Kullervo to herd the cattle with a loaf in which she had baked a stone, after praying to Ukko and the forest spirits to protect her herd.

object_literal: breaks his father's knife on the stone and turns wolves and bears into cattle
statement: Kalevala Rune XXXIII says Kullervo's father's knife, his only keepsake, broke on the stone in the loaf, and that on a crow's advice he let wolves and bears devour the herd and drove them home in the shape of cattle.

Kalevala Rune XXXIII says Ilmarinen's wife was mauled by the beasts when she went to milk them, that Kullervo refused to save her, reproaching her for the stone in his bread, and that he then fled into the forest.

Kalevala Rune XXXIV says an old woman in a blue robe told the fleeing Kullervo that his parents lived at the edge of Lapland, where he found them, and learned that his elder sister had vanished long ago while picking berries.

Kalevala Rune XXXV says Kullervo, useless at his father's work, was sent to pay the taxes, and on his way home lured a maiden into his sledge who next morning learned that she was Kalervo's lost daughter, his own sister.

object_literal: loses his sister to the rapids and resolves on vengeance
statement: Kalevala Rune XXXV says Kullervo's sister threw herself into the rapids when she learned the truth, and that Kullervo, though his mother begged him to live, resolved first to take vengeance on Untamo.

Kalevala Rune XXXVI says only Kullervo's mother promised to weep for him, that he wept only when told of her death, and that with a sword from Ukko he destroyed Untamo's clan and burned their dwellings.

Kalevala Rune XXXVI says Kullervo, finding his family dead, went with his dog to the place where he had wronged his sister, and after his sword answered that it would drink his guilty blood, fell upon it; Väinämöinen then warns against raising a child wrongly.

Kalevala Rune XXXIX says Väinämöinen persuaded Ilmarinen to go and win back the Sampo, that Ilmarinen forged him a sword adorned with the moon, the sun and the stars, and that they launched by song a war-boat that wept to go to war.
Kalevala Rune XXXIX says that Lemminkäinen, idle on a headland for want of war, hailed the boat and asked to come as the third hero, and that Väinämöinen took him aboard to go for the Sampo.

object_literal: kills the giant pike that holds the boat fast
statement: Kalevala Rune XL says the heroes' boat stuck on the back of a giant pike in the rapids, that Lemminkäinen and Ilmarinen failed to harm it, and that Väinämöinen pierced and lifted it with his sword.

Kalevala Rune XL says Väinämöinen made the first kantele from the giant pike's jawbone, with its teeth for pegs and hair from Hiisi's gelding for strings, and that no one else could draw a fair tune from it.

Kalevala Rune XLI says that when Väinämöinen played the kantele every creature came to listen — the beasts and Tapio of the forest, the birds, the fishes, Ahto king of the sea, and the daughters of the moon and sun, who dropped their spindles.

object_literal: weeps tears that become blue pearls
statement: Kalevala Rune XLI says that all who heard the kantele wept, and that Väinämöinen's own tears rolled into the sea, from which a blue duck brought them up changed into blue pearls.
Kalevala Rune XLII says Louhi refused to share the Sampo and called her warriors, and that Väinämöinen played the kantele until all the people of Pohjola fell asleep.

Kalevala Rune XLII says the heroes opened the copper mountain's doors by song, Ilmarinen buttering the hinges, and when Lemminkäinen could not lift the Sampo they ploughed through its roots with the great ox of Pohjola and carried it to their boat.

object_literal: sings against warning and wakes Pohjola through a crane
statement: Kalevala Rune XLII says that on the third day Lemminkäinen, against Väinämöinen's warning, burst into harsh song, and a startled crane flew screaming to Pohjola and woke its people, so that Louhi found the Sampo gone.

Kalevala Rune XLII says Louhi sent fog, which Väinämöinen cut with his sword, raised the sea monster Iku-Turso, which he banished by the ears, and called up a storm that swept his kantele into the sea.
Kalevala Rune XLIII says Louhi pursued the heroes as a giant eagle carrying her warriors, and that Väinämöinen smashed her talons with the rudder so that her warriors fell into the sea.

object_literal: shatters in the sea, enriching the sea and Kalevala
statement: Kalevala Rune XLIII says the Sampo fell from the boat as Louhi clutched it and shattered in the sea, its large pieces becoming the sea's riches and its small pieces drifting to Kalevala, where Väinämöinen planted them, while Louhi took home only the lid.

object_literal: comes into being among the first deities of High Heaven
statement: Kojiki Section I says that when heaven and earth began, Ame-no-minaka-nushi, Takami-musubi and Kami-musubi came into being in the Plain of High Heaven, and that while the land drifted like floating oil two more deities sprouted like a reed-shoot.
Kojiki Section II lists the Seven Divine Generations from Kuni-no-toko-tachi to the last pair, Izanagi and Izanami, counting each single deity and each pair as one generation.

Kojiki Section III says the heavenly deities gave Izanagi and Izanami a jewelled spear, and that brine dripping from its point as they stirred from the Floating Bridge of Heaven piled up into Onogoro Island.

object_literal: speaks first at the heavenly pillar, and a leech-child is born
statement: Kojiki Section IV says that after the two walked round the heavenly pillar and Izanami spoke first, their first child was a leech-child, put into a reed boat and floated away, and the island of Aha was not reckoned among their children.

Kojiki Section V says the heavenly deities' divination blamed the woman's speaking first, and that when Izanagi spoke first at the pillar the pair gave birth to the eight great islands, from Awaji to Ō-yamato-toyo-aki-tsu-shima.

object_literal: bears the deities of sea, mountains, wind and trees
statement: Kojiki Section VI says that after the islands Izanagi and Izanami bore many deities, among them the sea deity Ō-wata-tsu-mi, the mountain deity Ō-yama-tsu-mi, the Heavenly Bird-Boat and the food goddess Ō-ge-tsu-hime.

Kojiki Section VI says Izanami was burned in giving birth to the fire deity Kagutsuchi, that deities of metal, clay and water were born from her vomit, dung and urine as she lay sick, and that she then divinely retired.

Kojiki Sections VII–VIII say Izanagi mourned Izanami, buried her on Mount Hiba, and cut off Kagutsuchi's head with his ten-grasp sword, the blood near the guard becoming deities including Takemikazuchi.

Kojiki Section IX says Izanami told Izanagi she had eaten the food of Yomi and asked him not to look at her, and that when he lit a comb-tooth and looked he saw maggots and eight thunder deities on her body.

object_literal: escapes the pursuers of Yomi with grapes, bamboo shoots and three peaches
statement: Kojiki Section IX says Izanagi escaped the Ugly Females of Yomi by throwing down a head-dress that became grapes and a comb that became bamboo shoots, and drove back the thunder deities' host with three peaches at the foot of the Even Pass of Yomi.

Kojiki Section IX says that across the rock blocking the Even Pass of Yomi Izanami vowed to strangle a thousand people a day and Izanagi answered he would set up fifteen hundred birth-houses a day, and that Izanami was thereafter called the Great Deity of Yomi.

object_literal: purifies himself, and the three noble children are born of his washing
statement: Kojiki Section X says Izanagi purified himself at the river-mouth of Tachibana in Himuka, deities being born from his discarded clothing and his washing, and last Amaterasu from his left eye, Tsukuyomi from his right eye and Susanoo from his nose.

Kojiki Section XXXIII says that when the land was reported pacified, Ame-no-oshi-ho-mimi proposed his newborn son Ninigi in his place, and Amaterasu and Takagi-no-kami commanded Ninigi to descend and rule the Land of Fresh Rice-Ears.

Kojiki Section XXXIII says that a deity shining up to High Heaven and down to the Central Land stood at the heavenly crossroads, and when Ame-no-Uzume questioned him he named himself the earthly deity Sarutahiko, come to guide the August Grandchild.

Kojiki Section XXXIII says Amaterasu sent five chiefs of companies with Ninigi and gave him the curved jewels, the mirror and the Kusanagi sword, charging him to reverence the mirror as her own spirit.

object_literal: descends on the peak of Takachiho in Himuka
statement: Kojiki Sections XXXIII–XXXIV say Ninigi pushed through the eight-fold clouds and descended on the peak of Kuji-furu-take of Takachiho in Himuka, called the place exceedingly good, and built his palace there.

Kojiki Sections XXXV–XXXVI say Ame-no-Uzume escorted Sarutahiko home and took his name for the Duchesses of Saru, that Sarutahiko drowned when a shell caught his hand at Azaka, and that she slit the mouth of the sea-slug that would not answer.

Kojiki Section XXXVII says Ōyamatsumi sent both his daughters to Ninigi, and when Ninigi returned the ugly Iwanaga-hime and kept Konohana-sakuya-hime, he declared that the lives of the heavenly deity's descendants would be as brief as blossoms.
Kojiki Section XXXVIII says that when Ninigi doubted the child conceived in one night, Konohana-sakuya-hime gave birth inside a sealed, burning doorless hall to Hoderi, Hosuseri and Hoori.

Kojiki Section XXXIX says Hoori persuaded his brother Hoderi to exchange their gear, lost the fish-hook at sea, and could not make his brother accept five hundred or a thousand hooks forged from his sword in its place.

Kojiki Section XL says the salt deity Shio-tsuchi set Hoori in a tightly woven bamboo boat and told him to follow the current to the sea deity's palace built like fish-scales and sit in the cassia tree by its well.

Kojiki Section XL says Hoori spat a jewel into the vessel of Toyotama-bime's maid at the well, Toyotama-bime fell in love with him at sight, and the sea deity welcomed him on layered rugs and gave her to him in marriage.

Kojiki Sections XL–XLI say the sea deity found the hook in a sea-bream's throat, gave Hoori the tide-flowing and tide-ebbing jewels with counsel, and that Hoori used them to subdue Hoderi, who vowed to be his guard.

Kojiki Sections XLII–XLIII say Toyotama-bime gave birth in an unfinished hut thatched with cormorant feathers, was seen by Hoori in her true form as an eight-fathom wani, and in shame closed the sea-boundary and returned to the sea, leaving her son Ugaya-fuki-aezu.
Kojiki Section XX lists Susanoo's descendants and gives Ōkuninushi's five names: Ōkuninushi, Ōnamuji, Ashihara-shiko-wo, Yachihoko and Utsushi-kunitama.
