Kojiki Section XXI says Ōnamuji, carrying his brothers' bag, healed the hare of Inaba with fresh water and sedge pollen after the Eighty Deities had made its injuries worse, and the hare foretold that Princess Yakami would choose him.
Kojiki Section XXII says the Eighty Deities killed Ōnamuji by rolling down a red-hot boulder at Mount Tema, and Kami-musubi sent Princess Cockle-Shell and Princess Clam, who restored him to life.

Kojiki Section XXII says the Eighty Deities crushed Ōnamuji in a cleft tree, his mother restored him and sent him to Oho-ya-biko in Ki, who let him escape through the fork of a tree towards Susanoo's Nether-Distant-Land.
Kojiki Section XXIII says Suseri-bime married Ōnamuji when he arrived, and when Susanoo made him sleep in the snake room she gave him a snake-scarf to wave three times, so that he came out unharmed.

object_literal: gives her husband a scarf against centipedes and wasps
statement: Kojiki Section XXIII says that when Susanoo next put Ōnamuji in a room of centipedes and wasps, Suseri-bime again gave him a scarf against them and he came out unharmed.

Kojiki Section XXIII says that when Susanoo set fire to the moor around Ōnamuji, a mouse showed him a hollow in the ground to shelter in and brought back the whizzing arrow, and he presented the arrow to Susanoo.
Kojiki Section XXIII says that when Susanoo made Ōnamuji pick centipedes from his hair, Suseri-bime gave him muku berries and red earth to chew and spit, so that Susanoo fell asleep pleased with him.

Kojiki Section XXIII says Ōnamuji escaped with Suseri-bime and Susanoo's sword, bow and speaking lute, and Susanoo, pursuing to the Even Pass of Yomi, called on him to drive away his brothers, become Ōkuninushi and make Suseri-bime his chief wife.
Kojiki Sections XXIV–XXV say that as Yachihoko he wooed Princess Nunakawa of Koshi with songs, and that when Suseri-bime was jealous they exchanged songs and pledged each other with a wine-cup.

Kojiki Section XXVII says Sukuna-bikona came over the waves to Cape Miho in a seed-pod boat, Kami-musubi named him her child who slipped through her fingers, and he made the land with Ōkuninushi before crossing to the Eternal Land.

object_literal: enshrines the deity from the sea on Mount Mimoro
statement: Kojiki Section XXVIII says that after Sukuna-bikona left, a deity came over the sea illuminating it and offered to make the land with Ōkuninushi if worshipped on the eastern mountain of Yamato, the deity of Mount Mimoro.

Kojiki Sections XXX–XXXI say Ame-no-hohi and then Ame-no-Wakahiko failed to report from the Central Land, and that when Ame-no-Wakahiko shot the pheasant Naki-me, Takagi-no-kami threw the arrow back and it killed him on his bed.

Kojiki Section XXXII says Takemikazuchi, seated on an upturned sword on a wave at Inasa, demanded the land; Kotoshironushi agreed, Takeminakata was overpowered and fled to Suwa, and Ōkuninushi yielded the land on condition that a great palace be built for him.
Kojiki Section LXXIX says that when Keikō asked Wo-usu to teach his elder brother Oho-usu to come to meals, Wo-usu killed his brother, and the sovereign was afraid of his son's fierce heart.

Kojiki Section LXXX says Wo-usu, sent west against the Kumaso bravoes, took his aunt Yamato-hime's robe and skirt, let down his hair like a girl's and entered their housewarming feast, where they seated him between them.
Kojiki Section LXXX says Wo-usu killed both Kumaso bravoes at their feast, and that the dying younger brother, saying there was a braver man in Yamato than they, gave him the name Yamato Takeru.
Kojiki Section LXXXI says Yamato Takeru befriended the Izumo bravo, made a false wooden sword, exchanged swords with him after bathing in the river Hi, and killed him when he could not draw it.

Kojiki Section LXXXII says that when Yamato Takeru, sent east at once without troops, wept at Ise that his father wished him dead, his aunt Yamato-hime gave him the Kusanagi sword and a bag to open in an emergency.

Kojiki Section LXXXIII says that when the ruler of Sagamu set fire to the moor around him, Yamato Takeru opened his aunt's bag, mowed the grass with his sword and lit a counter-fire with the fire-striker, then killed the rulers, so that the place is called Yaizu.

Kojiki Section LXXXIV says that when the deity of the Hashirimizu strait raised waves against the boat, Oto-tachibana-hime spread rugs on the waves and entered the sea in Yamato Takeru's stead, the waves calmed, and seven days later her comb drifted ashore.

object_literal: sighs 'Azuma haya' on the Ashigara pass, naming the East
statement: Kojiki Section LXXXV says Yamato Takeru killed the deity of the Ashigara pass, which came as a white deer, with a wild chive, and on the pass sighed three times 'Azuma haya', so that the land is called Azuma.

object_literal: completes a verse with an old fire-keeper at Sakaori
statement: Kojiki Section LXXXVI says that at the palace of Sakaori in Kai, when Yamato Takeru asked in verse how many nights had passed since Niibari and Tsukuba, an old fire-keeper answered nine nights and ten days, and was made ruler of the East.

Kojiki Sections LXXXVII–LXXXVIII say Yamato Takeru married Miyazu-hime, left the Kusanagi sword with her and went bare-handed against Mount Ibuki, where he took the deity in the form of a white boar for its messenger and was struck senseless by hail.

object_literal: names the places of his last journey as his strength fails
statement: Kojiki Section LXXXIX says Yamato Takeru, weakened, named the Awakening Spring, Tagi and the Staff Slope, found his forgotten sword still under the pine of Cape Otsu, and at Mie said his legs were like a thrice-bent rice cake.

object_literal: dies at Nobo and turns into a great white bird
statement: Kojiki Sections LXXXIX–XC say Yamato Takeru died at Nobo after singing of his longing for Yamato and of the sword left by the maiden's bed, and that he turned into a great white bird that flew towards the shore, stopped at Shiki and rose into the sky again.

Mahābhārata, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavat-yana Parva) says Kṛṣṇa went to Hastināpura as the Pāṇḍavas' envoy and asked for half the kingdom or even five villages, and that Duryodhana refused to yield even as much land as a needle's point.

Mahābhārata, Bhishma Parva (Bhagavat-Gita Parva) says Arjuna, seeing his kin and teachers in the opposing army, laid down his bow, and that Kṛṣṇa, his charioteer, spoke to him between the armies in the discourse known as the Bhagavad Gītā, after which he took up his bow.

Mahābhārata, Bhishma Parva (Bhishma-vadha Parva) says that on the tenth day Bhīṣma, refusing to strike at Śikhaṇḍin, fell beneath Arjuna's arrows onto a bed of arrows, where Arjuna gave him a pillow of arrows and water from the earth, and he chose to await the sun's northern course before dying.

Mahābhārata, Drona Parva (Abhimanyu-vadha Parva) says the young Abhimanyu, knowing how to enter Droṇa's circular array but not how to leave it, broke in while Jayadratha held back the other Pāṇḍavas, and was killed by several warriors together.

object_literal: vows to kill Jayadratha before sunset and fulfils the vow
statement: Mahābhārata, Drona Parva (Pratijna and Jayadratha-vadha Parvas) says Arjuna vowed to kill Jayadratha before sunset or enter the fire, and that when Kṛṣṇa darkened the sun and Jayadratha showed himself, Arjuna struck off his head and sent it into his father's lap.

object_literal: spends Indra's dart on Ghaṭotkaca
statement: Mahābhārata, Drona Parva (Ghatotkacha-vadha Parva) says that in the night battle Karṇa, begged by Duryodhana, spent the one-time dart from Indra that he had kept for Arjuna on Bhīma's rākṣasa son Ghaṭotkaca, and that Kṛṣṇa rejoiced that Arjuna was saved.

Mahābhārata, Drona Parva (Drona-vadha Parva) says that after Bhīma killed an elephant named Aśvatthāman, Yudhiṣṭhira told Droṇa that Aśvatthāman was dead, adding 'the elephant' under his breath; his chariot touched the ground, and Droṇa laid down his arms and was slain by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

Mahābhārata, Karna Parva says that on the seventeenth day Karṇa's chariot wheel sank into the earth through a brahmin's curse, that Kṛṣṇa answered his appeal to dharma by recalling Draupadī and Abhimanyu, and that Arjuna struck off his head.

Mahābhārata, Shalya Parva (Hrada-pravesa Parva) says that after Śalya and Śakuni were slain Duryodhana fled and hid beneath a lake, and that when Yudhiṣṭhira offered single combat with any of the five for the kingdom he rose to fight with the mace, and Bhīma met him.

Mahābhārata, Shalya Parva (Gada-yuddha Parva) says that, prompted by a sign from Arjuna recalling his vow, Bhīma broke Duryodhana's thighs with his mace against the rules of the duel, angering Balarāma, while flowers fell from heaven on the fallen king.

Mahābhārata, Sauptika Parva says Aśvatthāman, inspired by an owl killing sleeping crows, raided the Pāṇḍava camp by night and killed Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin and Draupadī's five sons in the sleeping camp, and that the dying Duryodhana was content on hearing it.

Mahābhārata, Sauptika Parva (Aishika Parva) says that when Aśvatthāman, overtaken, loosed the Brahmaśiras weapon and turned it on the Pāṇḍavas' unborn heirs, Kṛṣṇa cursed him to wander for three thousand years, and he gave up the jewel on his forehead.

object_literal: is the subject of the tale told to the exiled Yudhiṣṭhira
statement: Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section LII says that when the exiled Yudhiṣṭhira lamented that no king was more unfortunate, the sage Bṛhadaśva offered to tell him of Nala, who also lost his kingdom at dice and regained it.
Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section LIII says Nala and Damayantī came to love each other through report, and that a golden-winged swan released by Nala carried praise of each to the other.
Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section LIV says Indra, Agni, Varuṇa and Yama, going to Damayantī's svayaṃvara, met Nala and bound him by his promise to be their messenger to her.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Sections LV–LVI say Nala, made invisible by the gods, delivered their suit to Damayantī, who answered that her heart was his and that she would choose him before the gods so that he would not break his word.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section LVII says that at the svayaṃvara the four gods took Nala's form, and that when Damayantī prayed they showed the marks of gods — no sweat, unblinking eyes, unfaded garlands, feet not touching the ground — so that she chose the real Nala.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Sections LVII–LVIII say the gods gave Nala boons and he lived happily with Damayantī, but Kali, angered that she had chosen a mortal, resolved to enter Nala and ruin him with Dvāpara's help in the dice.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Sections LIX–LXI say Kali entered Nala after twelve years when he prayed without washing his feet, that Nala then lost everything at dice to Pushkara despite all pleading, and that Damayantī sent their children to Vidarbha before following him out of the city.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Sections LXI–LXII say the dice, in the shape of golden birds, carried off Nala's last garment, and that at midnight in a rest-house he cut away half of the sleeping Damayantī's garment and, driven by Kali, abandoned her.

object_literal: survives the forest and finds refuge at the Chedi court
statement: Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Sections LXIII–LXV say the abandoned Damayantī was saved from a python by a hunter whom she cursed to death when he threatened her, survived a stampede that destroyed a caravan, and was taken in at the Chedi court.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section LXVI says Nala carried the nāga Karkoṭaka out of a forest fire, that Karkoṭaka bit him at the tenth step and changed his form so that he would not be known, and sent him to King Ṛtuparṇa of Ayodhyā as the charioteer Bāhuka.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Sections LXVII–LXX say the brahmin Sudeva found Damayantī at the Chedi court by her mole, and that the words she sent out after Nala drew a sighing answer from Ṛtuparṇa's charioteer Bāhuka, reported by the brahmin Parṇāda.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Sections LXXI–LXXII say Ṛtuparṇa raced to Damayantī's announced second svayaṃvara with Bāhuka driving, and at a Vibhītaka tree taught him the science of dice in exchange for horse-lore, whereupon Kali left Nala, vomiting Karkoṭaka's venom.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Sections LXXIII–LXXVI say Damayantī tested Bāhuka through her maid Keśinī, knew him by his cooking and his tears for their children, and that when the wind god attested her faithfulness Nala resumed his true form.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Sections LXXVII–LXXIX say Nala returned to Nishadha, won back his kingdom from Pushkara in a single throw with the science of dice, forgave his brother, and that Bṛhadaśva then taught the science of dice to Yudhiṣṭhira.

object_literal: is visited by the goddess Sāvitrī after eighteen years of devotion
statement: Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section CCXCI says that when Yudhiṣṭhira asked Mārkaṇḍeya about a woman as virtuous as Draupadī, the sage told of childless King Aśvapati of Madra, to whom the goddess Sāvitrī appeared from the sacrificial fire after eighteen years of vows and offerings.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section CCXCI says the goddess, by Brahmā's will, promised Aśvapati a radiant daughter instead of the sons he asked for, and that the child born to his queen was named Sāvitrī after her.
Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section CCXCI says that because no one dared to seek the radiant Sāvitrī in marriage, her father sent her out with old ministers to choose a husband for herself.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section CCXCII says Sāvitrī chose Satyavān, son of the blind, exiled King Dyumatsena, and that the sage Nārada praised Satyavān's virtues but foretold that he would die a year from that day.

object_literal: refuses to choose again though Satyavān is fated to die
statement: Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section CCXCII says Sāvitrī refused to choose another husband, saying a daughter is given in marriage only once, and that Nārada advised Aśvapati to give her to Satyavān.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section CCXCIII says Aśvapati gave Sāvitrī in marriage to Satyavān at Dyumatsena's forest hermitage, and that she put aside her ornaments for bark garments and served her husband's parents.

object_literal: keeps a three-night vow before the foretold day
statement: Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section CCXCIV says that with four days left before Satyavān's foretold death Sāvitrī kept a three-night vow standing without food or drink, and on the fourth day accepted the elders' blessing that she would never be widowed.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section CCXCIV says that on the fated day Sāvitrī, with her husband's parents' leave, went with Satyavān into the forest, smiling at the sights he showed her while she watched him as one about to die.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section CCXCV says that as Satyavān lay with his head in Sāvitrī's lap, Yama, red-clad and crowned with a noose in his hand, came himself because of Satyavān's virtue and drew out his thumb-sized soul.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section CCXCV says Sāvitrī followed Yama, invoking the friendship of seven steps and speaking of dharma, and that the pleased Yama granted her first boon, the restoration of her blind father-in-law's sight and strength.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section CCXCV says Yama granted Sāvitrī further boons — her father-in-law's kingdom, a hundred sons for her father and a hundred sons by Satyavān — and, since the last could not be fulfilled without Satyavān, loosened his noose and restored her husband.

Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Section CCXCVI says Satyavān woke in Sāvitrī's lap as from a long sleep, wept for his anxious parents, and that she supported him and carried his axe as they returned through the forest at night.

object_literal: regains his sight and his kingdom through Sāvitrī's boons
statement: Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Sections CCXCVI–CCXCVII say Dyumatsena regained his sight that day, Sāvitrī told the hermitage of Yama and the boons, and the next morning ministers of Śālva announced the usurper's death and recalled Dyumatsena to his throne.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('The March into Mazinderan'), says Kay Kāvus, enchanted by a demon disguised as a minstrel singing of Māzandarān, resolved to conquer it, and his alarmed champions sent for Zāl.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('The March into Mazinderan'), says that when Kay Kāvus, scorning Zāl's warning, ravaged Māzandarān, the White Demon brought darkness and a storm of stones and hail that blinded the shah and his army, who were taken captive.

object_literal: kills a lion while Rostam sleeps in the first stage
statement: The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('The March into Mazinderan'), says Rostam chose the short, perilous road to Māzandarān, and that on the first night, as he slept, Rakhsh killed a lion that attacked them, for which Rostam scolded him.

object_literal: is led to water by a ram in the desert
statement: The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('The March into Mazinderan'), says that in the second stage Rostam, fainting with thirst in the desert, prayed to God and was led by a ram to a spring.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('The March into Mazinderan'), says that in the third stage Rakhsh three times woke Rostam to a dragon that hid itself by magic, and that when Rostam finally saw it Rakhsh bit the dragon and Rostam cut off its head.

object_literal: unmasks and kills a witch by naming God
statement: The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('The March into Mazinderan'), says that in the fourth stage a witch disguised as a beautiful girl joined Rostam at a feast, and that when he named God she turned back into a hag and he killed her.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('The March into Mazinderan'), says that in the fifth stage Rostam, after tearing off the ears of a field-keeper who struck him, defeated and lassoed the local lord Olād and made him his guide with the promise of Māzandarān's throne.

object_literal: tears off the head of the demon Arzhang
statement: The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('The March into Mazinderan'), says that in the sixth stage Rostam rode alone into the camp of the demon Arzhang, tore off his head and flung it among the demons, who fled in terror.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('The March into Mazinderan'), says that in the seventh stage Rostam entered the White Demon's cave at noon when the demons slept, woke the demon rather than strike him sleeping, and after a desperate fight killed him and tore out his liver.
The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('The March into Mazinderan'), says the blood of the White Demon's liver, dropped by Rostam into the eyes of Kay Kāvus and his champions, restored their sight.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('The March into Mazinderan'), says that when the king of Māzandarān turned himself into a rock in battle, Rostam carried the rock to the Iranian camp and threatened it until the king came out, and that Olād was then made ruler of Māzandarān.

object_literal: tries to fly to heaven on an eagle-drawn throne and falls
statement: The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Kai Kaous Committeth More Follies'), says that, tempted by a demon to rule the sky, Kay Kāvus tried to fly on a throne drawn by hungry eagles straining after meat on spears, fell into a forest, and was found and rebuked by Rostam and the champions.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem and Sohrab'), says Rakhsh was stolen by Turanian riders while Rostam slept after hunting on the border, and that Rostam tracked him to Samangān, whose king welcomed him as a guest.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem and Sohrab'), says Tahmineh, princess of Samangān, came to Rostam's chamber by night, told him she had long loved him and wished to bear his son, and that Rostam then asked the king for her hand and married her.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem and Sohrab'), says Rostam, leaving Samangān, gave Tahmineh an armlet to bind on their son's arm if a son were born, and that she bore Sohrāb and bound it on him.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem and Sohrab'), says Sohrāb grew wondrously fast, learned from Tahmineh that Rostam was his father, and resolved to invade Iran, overthrow Kay Kāvus and set Rostam on the throne.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem and Sohrab'), says Afrāsiyāb sent the generals Hūmān and Bārmān with an army to support Sohrāb, secretly charging them to keep father and son from knowing each other so that one might kill the other.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem and Sohrab'), says the warrior maiden Gordāfarid rode out against Sohrāb from the White Castle, was revealed when he knocked off her helmet, and escaped him with a false promise before the castle's people fled by a secret way.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem and Sohrab'), says Kay Kāvus summoned Rostam against the young invader, raged at his delay and ordered him hanged, and that Rostam rode off in anger until Gūdarz persuaded him that he would be thought afraid.

object_literal: kills Zende-razm unknowing while spying in the Turanian camp
statement: The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem and Sohrab'), says Rostam, spying in the Turanian camp, unknowingly killed Tahmineh's brother Zende-razm, who was to point him out to Sohrāb, and that the captive Hajīr lied to Sohrāb that Rostam was not with the army.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem and Sohrab'), says that on the first day Sohrāb asked his opponent whether he was Rostam, son of Zāl, that Rostam denied it, and that they fought with spears, swords and maces till evening without a victor.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem and Sohrab'), says that on the second day Sohrāb threw Rostam and was about to kill him, but Rostam claimed an Iranian custom that a foe may be slain only at the second fall, and Sohrāb let him go.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem and Sohrab'), says Rostam prayed for the return of the strength he had once asked God to lessen, and on the third day threw Sohrāb and stabbed him, whereupon the dying Sohrāb said his father Rostam would avenge him.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem and Sohrab'), says Rostam recognised his dying son by the armlet he had left with Tahmineh, that Kay Kāvus withheld the healing elixir, and that Sohrāb died, Rostam carried him home, and Tahmineh died of grief within a year.
The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Zal'), says Sām, ashamed that his newborn son had white hair and fearing he would be called a demon's child, had the baby exposed on Mount Alborz.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Zal'), says the Simorgh carried the exposed baby to her nest on Alborz to feed her young but, moved to pity, raised him with them until he grew into a youth seen by passing caravans.

object_literal: repents after two dreams and seeks his son on Mount Alborz
statement: The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Zal'), says Sām, rebuked in two dreams and by his priests for casting off his son, repented, went to Mount Alborz, and prayed to the Creator to be given him back.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Zal'), says the Simorgh returned Zāl to his father, naming him Dastān and giving him a feather to burn in danger, and that the king's astrologers foretold his greatness.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Zal and Rudabeh'), says Zāl and Rūdābeh, daughter of King Mehrāb of Kābul, a descendant of Zahhāk, fell in love through report, and that Rūdābeh's maidens agreed to help her.
The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Zal and Rudabeh'), says Rūdābeh let down her long hair from her tower for Zāl to climb, but he climbed by his lasso instead, and they vowed to marry no one else.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Zal and Rudabeh'), says Sām, after the astrologers foretold a mighty hero from the match, was willing, but King Manūchehr, fearing Zahhāk's blood, ordered him to march against Mehrāb's Kābul.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Zal and Rudabeh'), says Queen Sindokht stopped Mehrāb from killing their daughter and went herself with gifts to the advancing Sām, who, moved by her wisdom, swore to spare Kābul and bring about the marriage.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Zal and Rudabeh'), says Zāl answered the riddles of Manūchehr's wise men — the twelve cypresses as the months, the black and white horses as night and day, the mower in the garden as death — and won the king's consent.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Zal and Rudabeh'), says Zāl and Rūdābeh were married with great festivities in Kābul in Sām's presence and returned to Zābulistān, which Sām gave into Zāl's rule.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem'), says that when Rūdābeh could not give birth, Zāl burned the Simorgh's feather and the Simorgh instructed that she be drugged and the child drawn from her side, and that she named the child Rostam from her cry of deliverance.

The Shahnameh, as retold by Zimmern ('Rustem'), says the young Rostam killed a raging white elephant with one blow of Sām's mace and lassoed the rose-dappled colt Rakhsh, whose price the herdsman said was the land of Iran.

Soushen ji juan 1 says Dong Yong sold himself to bury his father, and that the woman who became his wife wove a hundred bolts of silk in ten days to repay his master, revealed herself as the Weaving Maiden sent by the Lord of Heaven for his filial piety, and rose into the sky.
tradition_scope: Soushen ji (Gan Bao, received twenty-juan text)

statement: Soushen ji juan 11 says the swordsmith Gan Jiang, foreseeing that the king of Chu would kill him for taking three years, brought only the female sword and left word that the male sword lay behind a pine on a stone, which his son Chi Bi found behind the pine pillar of the hall.
tradition_scope: Soushen ji (Gan Bao, received twenty-juan text)

object_literal: gives his head and sword to a stranger to avenge his father
statement: Soushen ji juan 11 says Chi Bi gave his own head and sword to a stranger, who boiled the head before the king of Chu, cut off the king's head into the cauldron and then his own, so that the three heads were buried together as the Tomb of the Three Kings.
tradition_scope: Soushen ji (Gan Bao, received twenty-juan text)

object_literal: keeps a promise across a thousand li and attends his dead friend's burial
statement: Soushen ji juan 11 says Fan Juqing kept his two-year promise to visit Zhang Yuanbo, and that after Zhang's death a dream summoned him to the burial, where the coffin would not move until he came and bade his friend farewell.
tradition_scope: Soushen ji (Gan Bao, received twenty-juan text)

object_literal: tells of the wrongly executed filial widow of Donghai and the three years' drought
statement: Soushen ji juan 11 says a filial widow of Donghai was falsely condemned for her mother-in-law's suicide, that three years of drought followed until a new governor sacrificed at her grave, and adds the elders' tale that her blood flowed up the bamboo pole as she had sworn.
tradition_scope: Soushen ji (Gan Bao, received twenty-juan text)

object_literal: dies with his wife rather than be parted, and their graves grow the Trees of Longing
statement: Soushen ji juan 11 says that after King Kang of Song took Han Ping's wife, both husband and wife took their own lives, and that from their separate graves grew catalpas whose roots and branches intertwined, with a pair of mandarin ducks in them, called the Trees of Longing.
tradition_scope: Soushen ji (Gan Bao, received twenty-juan text)

object_literal: steals the elixir and becomes the toad in the moon
statement: Soushen ji juan 14 says Heng'e stole the drug of deathlessness that Yi had obtained from the Queen Mother of the West, consulted the diviner Youhuang, who called the journey auspicious, and entrusted herself to the moon, becoming the toad.
tradition_scope: Soushen ji (Gan Bao, received twenty-juan text)

object_literal: tells how a girl and a horse's hide became the first silkworms
statement: Soushen ji juan 14 tells that a girl promised in jest to marry the horse if it brought her father home, that her father shot the horse, and that its hide carried her off and both turned into silkworms in a tree thereafter called sang, the mulberry.

object_literal: tells of the feather-robed woman whose robe was hidden
